  source files and TypeScript source aliases alone do not expose a package API;
  `node --test scripts/internal-api-calendar-exports.test.js` exercises Contacts'
  real ESM resolution for the Calendar series clients without local builds
- run `vercel pull`
- run `vercel build`
- deploy prebuilt artifacts for satellite apps and the hosted platform
  production workflow
- treat `vercel-preview-platform.yaml` as platform build validation only;
  self-hosted machines own their own Docker `apps/web` runtime deployment
- serialize production runs through their existing per-workflow, per-branch
  concurrency groups with cancellation disabled and `queue: max`; later pushes
  and recovery dispatches wait rather than interrupting active deployments
- record non-blocking GitHub Deployment markers after successful Vercel preview
  builds and production deploys so the next production push can evaluate every
  change since the last successful run

The platform preview workflow can cross-credit a successful same-SHA production
platform build marker. Production does not cross-credit preview markers because
it must build and deploy the prebuilt production artifacts. This only applies to
the platform workflows; satellite Vercel workflows still build and deploy
independently.

### Database automation

- `supabase-staging.yaml`
- `supabase-production.yaml`

These cover staging schema promotion and production schema promotion.

Database workflows that install the Supabase CLI use
`.github/actions/setup-supabase-cli-with-retry` after checkout with Node 20+ and
npm available. The wrapper pins setup-cli v3.0.1 to its reviewed commit and passes
the exact stable CLI version resolved for `apps/database` in the root `bun.lock`.
A missing or malformed pin fails before installation; there is no `latest`
fallback. Explicit overrides must be exact stable versions. The v3 action no
longer accepts `github-token`, so callers do not pass a token.

The installer gets a runner-temporary home to protect any existing Bun binary.
An always-running restoration step verifies that binary's version and restores
its PATH priority, while retaining the installed CLI path. Jobs without an
existing Bun runtime keep the installer's runtime. Four attempts use 5, 10 and
20-second backoff; a fourth failure still fails the job. Real installer and
follow-on runtime behavior must pass the owning exact-commit CI jobs before
integration; this does not authorize a migration dispatch.

The Supabase baseline contract captures child output privately because startup
can print local credentials. Its failure summary forwards only fixed categories:
image pull throttling or transport exhaustion, migration failure, service health
failure, timeout, or output-buffer exhaustion. Other failures retain the generic
diagnostic instruction. Never print the raw child error, stdout, or stderr to CI.
Active Supabase-starting jobs run `.github/actions/cache-supabase-images` after
the owning dependency install. Image versions come from the installed pinned CLI's
`services -o json`, which includes local version overrides. CLI 2.121.0 omits Kong,
Mailpit and imgproxy there; the helper carries their reviewed Dockerfile pins
(2.8.1, v1.31.3 and v3.26.0) and rejects a different CLI until those pins are
reviewed. Catalog entries take precedence over fallback pins, including local
overrides; repeated catalog image names fail rather than silently choosing a tag. Registry rewriting
matches the CLI, including `postgrest/postgrest` becoming `supabase/postgrest`.

The exact image list, registry, OS and architecture form the SHA256 cache key;
there are no prefix restores. A hit loads the Docker archive and inspects every
expected image before startup. The baseline restore also inspects its already
loaded Postgres image instead of pulling it unconditionally. The CLI inspects
local images before its pull path. A miss pulls each missing image with at most
three attempts, 2/4-second backoff plus bounded jitter, 90-second command limits
and a two-minute total pull deadline. Failure stops before database startup,
including in the 15-minute cross-runner restore job. It never replays SQL tests,
resets or pushes. Fixed exhaustion summaries include only the known registry host
and untagged image name, never raw captured diagnostics or credentials.

Contract jobs cache five images: Postgres, postgres-meta for type generation, and
GoTrue/Realtime/Storage for fresh-database migration containers. The CLI runs those
three bootstrap containers even with their long-running services excluded. The
HTTP contract adds Kong and PostgREST; the full profile caches ten configured
images, excluding disabled edge runtime, analytics and pooling. Archives have a
6 GiB hard bound, checked before save from image sizes and again on the tar file
before save/load. Missing images or an oversized archive fail visibly.

Only `push` and `workflow_dispatch` on `refs/heads/main` save archives. PRs and
other branches restore only; no PR-scoped uploads duplicate these large caches.
Until a trusted cache exists, PR jobs still require successful registry pulls.
Once this workflow is present on main, the release owner can bootstrap all three
exact profile keys without starting database contracts:

```sh
gh workflow run supabase-baseline.yaml --ref main -f seed_images_only=true
```

Seed profiles use `fail-fast: false`, so a throttled profile cannot cancel the
remaining profiles. On an exact profile miss, seeds and normal PR jobs restore
the exact contract key when its image set is a strict subset of the requested
profile, load and inspect it, then pull only locally missing images. The subset
key uses the same image/registry/OS/architecture identity; no prefix fallback is
used. A trusted save still archives the complete requested image set. Serial
matrix execution allows reuse of an already completed contract seed; matrix
ordering is not a dependency guarantee, so rerun the dispatch after a partial seed.

That main-only dispatch allows seven attempts within a ten-minute total pull
budget per profile and retains 15-minute job limits. Only this trusted Linux x64
seed path can substitute one existing retry slot after an ECR throttle with an
anonymous pull from a source-allowlisted official `ghcr.io/supabase/*` publication.
The allowlist covers every image in the current CLI 2.117.0 and fixed CLI 2.121.0
seed profiles:

| Image | CLI 2.117.0 tag | CLI 2.121.0 tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| gotrue | v2.196.0 | v2.197.0 |
| imgproxy | v3.8.0 | v3.26.0 |
| kong | 2.8.1 | 2.8.1 |
| mailpit | v1.30.2 | v1.31.3 |
| postgres-meta | v0.99.0 | v0.100.0 |
| postgres | 17.6.1.167 | 17.11.0.004 |
| postgrest | v16.2 | v16.4 |
| realtime | v2.130.0 | v2.143.4 |
| storage-api | v1.72.1 | v1.82.1 |
| studio | 2026.08.24-sha-8ec45b2 | 2026.10.12-sha-3699278 |

All 19 unique tags have equal ECR/GHCR OCI index, linux/amd64 manifest and config
digests. No image in these seed profiles remains ECR-only. Edge-runtime, Logflare,
Vector and Supavisor are outside both seed profiles because edge runtime,
analytics and pooling are disabled; their publication identity is not qualified
here. Do not enable those services or expand cache keys to obtain a fallback.
Unlisted tags remain ECR-only.

Pulls use the pinned linux/amd64 manifest digest and verify Docker's RepoDigests,
config ID, OS and architecture before tagging the canonical ECR reference.
A fallback must agree with a supplied canonical platform/config pin before its
pull. Alternate transport failure or identity mismatch stops the seed without
retrying or tagging. Archives retain the unchanged canonical ECR-tag cache key.
There is no login, additional attempt budget, arbitrary registry input or PR path.

Regenerate the metadata using only anonymous registry manifest GETs:

```sh
node scripts/ci/supabase-image-cache-registry.js > /tmp/supabase-image-publications.json
```

This helper reads the two pinned upstream CLI Dockerfiles, selects only the ten
seed-profile services (excluding alternate Postgres major versions), queries
ECR/GHCR tags and linux/amd64 manifests, hashes the returned bytes and records
config digests. It never pulls image layers, logs in, changes source data or runs
Docker. Each metadata request has a 30-second timeout and at most three attempts
for HTTP 429/5xx. A missing publication, metadata error or content mismatch exits
nonzero; resolve it before qualifying an image. Compare both registries' `amd64`
and `config` fields, then copy the qualified GHCR `index`, `amd64`, `config` and
fixed repository into `scripts/ci/supabase-image-cache-seed-data.json` fallbacks.
For fixed catalogs, retain matching canonical pins. Index equality is recorded
for these tags; platform/config equality is the runtime identity requirement.
If content differs or a public GHCR publication is absent, leave that image
ECR-only and document it. Never replace a failed comparison with a tag-only pull.
Run the image-cache, seed and registry tests after changing the data.

PR cache misses keep their existing ECR-only pull policy. Credentialless,
digest-pinned read-only fallback is a possible separate change, but must first
review allowlist provenance in PR-controlled checkouts, keep the two-minute
budget and terminal verification, and enforce no cache writes or added privileges.
Removing the trusted-seed guard alone does not preserve the current trust model.

For premerge CLI 2.121.0 cache preparation, the owner may select the fixed
`seed_image_catalog=cli-2.121.0` dispatch choice together with
`seed_images_only=true` on main. This reads reviewed source data without running
the future CLI or checking out PR code. Every catalog image is pulled by its
reviewed ECR linux/amd64 manifest digest, verified before save, and tagged with
the original ECR version reference. The exact tag list still goes through the
existing key function; the catalog does not change consumer keys, archive paths
or registry identity. An absent selector or `current` retains installed-CLI
metadata and supplemental version validation. The fixed catalog is Linux x64
only and requires the existing trusted 600-second seed mode. Update source
catalogs only after reviewing the upstream CLI list and anonymous index/platform
manifest metadata, including platform config digests; never accept a caller list.

GitHub's cache scope allows PRs to read main caches. Cache retention is shared
with Flutter SDK and Bun archives; capacity pressure can evict previously seeded
images. Before another owner-controlled seed, inspect the exact cache inventory
and active runs rather than assuming more retries establish retention. Acceptance
requires exact producer key/ref/size evidence, a fresh consumer's exact hit and
successful runtime contracts, then retained entries after the ordinary CI wave.
Source tests and registry metadata parity do not establish hosted alternate
transport reachability or runtime success. Exact-head hosted CI remains required.

### Repository cache budget

The repository's 10 GiB Actions cache budget uses least-recently-used eviction.
Cache misses can make Supabase contracts depend on throttled public ECR pulls.
Keep heavyweight writes on trusted refs; PRs restore the main cache rather than
creating a copy under every merge ref. This reduces eviction pressure but does
not reserve capacity or guarantee image retention.

| Cache family | Observed pressure | Save policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Supabase images | About 1.1 GiB and 717 MiB per observed profile | Main push/dispatch only; exact image keys |
| Android Gradle | Previous broad archive reached 4.29 GB | Only wrapper distributions and module downloads; skip saves above 512 MiB; one main-push producer |
| Flutter SDK/pub | SDK archives can exceed 1 GiB | Shared wrapper restores on every ref and saves on main push/dispatch; SDK/pub identities use platform and release, without lockfile generations |
| Bun downloads | About 1 GiB per observed Linux archive | Main push/dispatch only; one v2 archive per OS, architecture and pinned Bun version |
| CocoaPods | About 82 MiB per observed iOS PR copy | Explicit restore everywhere; save only on main pushes, including macOS pods |

These are incident measurements, not fixed sizes or a guaranteed total. Gradle
uses one `gradle-downloads-v2-<OS>-<arch>-java17` entry per platform, without
build-file hashes or fallback to `gradle-v1-`. Only `mobile-build-android.yaml`
saves it, after `scripts/ci/gradle-cache-budget.js` measures the selected paths
with archive header/padding allowance. Empty or over-budget trees skip saving;
builds retain their local downloads. Transforms, build caches, daemon and native
state stay out of the archive. A restored immutable entry may lack newer modules;
Gradle downloads those normally. Pub downloads similarly use `flutter-pub-v2-`
platform/channel/release keys; `pub get` still resolves each checked-in lockfile.
Changing a lockfile does not need a new archive of the entire download store.

After this policy merges, an operator should remove the obsolete `gradle-v1-`
entries, and obsolete lock-hashed Flutter pub entries once the v2 entries are
available. Inspect live usage before reseeding: leave room for every selected
Supabase profile, not just the first archive. Dispatch the main-only Supabase
image seed described below, verify its saves, then verify a contract consumer
reports a cache hit without registry pulls. Do not delete active SDK, Bun,
Supabase or CodeQL entries as routine cleanup. Old mobile workflows already
running at pre-policy commits may still save old keys; drain those before cleanup.
No cache is deleted or seed dispatched by this policy change. The Gradle gate
bounds its selected uncompressed bytes to 512 MiB; hosted archive sizes and the
aggregate footprint still require the read-only storage report. Flutter releases
and Supabase profiles can overlap, so this is not a reserved capacity guarantee.

PRs cannot warm missing heavyweight caches. The static budget gates are
`node --test scripts/ci/heavyweight-cache-budget.test.js scripts/ci/mobile-cache-budget.test.js`, also discovered by
`bun test:scripts`. The inventory covers every save-capable cache action and setup cache input in
workflows and composites, checking trusted and untrusted events/refs. Combined `actions/cache` still registers a post-job save when
`lookup-only` is enabled, so it remains in the inventory. Unknown keys and paths
have no implicit exemption. The explicit exceptions compare the complete input
set and workflow/job: small E2E proof JSON, the MCP tooling pip download cache,
Discord's pruned, lockfile-scoped uv downloads, and Buildx executable binaries.
Rust Cargo saves and BuildKit layer exports are explicitly inventoried as paused
source, with switchboard or job-fence checks and an exact scope list. These are
not claims that retained archives are small or safe to reactivate. Each exception
has a recorded reason; expanding paths, inputs or export scopes requires review.

Production mobile jobs only restore the Gradle/Pods caches populated by main
builds. They register no unreachable main-push saves. The paused Docker E2E jobs
reuse the exact shared `full` Supabase image profile instead of writing a second
`supabase-docker-v2` archive of every locally present tag. The registry benchmark
choice and all pause gates remain in place; this source change does not resume
Docker or establish hosted runtime acceptance. Only these E2E image-warming
steps continue after a cache or bounded pull failure, allowing baseline/startup
to pull any missing images. Only general Playwright shard 1 may create and upload
an archive on trusted main runs; other shards and the cross-app job restore
without saving. The shared action's `save` input defaults to true, preserving
strict contract producers. Allowlisted configuration errors, including enabled
uncached services, emit a warning annotation and step-summary line before the
helper fails; E2E fallback does not hide that diagnostic. Raw CLI errors remain
suppressed. Contract workflows keep strict image-cache setup.

The same-day result planner may reuse shard 1's proof and leave a run without a seeder; its fingerprint covers every image-key input, so input changes invalidate that proof, and a manual `supabase-baseline` dispatch with `seed_images_only=true` provides the fallback.

Bun dependencies use `bun-deps-v2-<OS>-<architecture>-<pinned Bun version>`
without a lockfile hash or prefix fallback. This chooses a coarser immutable
archive over automatic deletion: lockfile changes cannot create new multi-GiB
archives or race a cleanup job, and no write-scoped API token or cleanup loop is
needed. Bun still resolves the current lockfile and fetches missing packages;
newly added downloads do not enter the archive until the pinned Bun version
changes. This cache therefore drifts behind `bun.lock`: an exact key hit does
not mean every current dependency is cached, and newly added packages can be
downloaded on each run until the Bun version changes. Review a deliberate cache
namespace refresh if a long-lived Bun pin makes this repeated work material;
there is no scheduled writer or automatic refresh. Install correctness remains
bound to the current lockfile.
The runtime binary uses `bun-runtime-v2-<OS>-<architecture>-<pinned Bun version>`
with no lockfile hash or restore prefix: a lockfile change does not change the
pinned executable. Old v1 archives receive no
restores from v2 and age out under LRU; the first trusted v2 warmup and coexistence
with old entries can still cause eviction. No immediate space reclamation is
claimed. After confirming that no workflow or action pins Bun 1.4.3, the release owner can perform this
one-time cleanup without adding a scheduled maintenance loop:

```sh
rg -n '1\.4\.3' .github/workflows .github/actions --glob '*.yml' --glob '*.yaml'
gh cache list --repo tutur3u/platform --key bun-deps-v1- --limit 1000 --json id,key,ref,sizeInBytes
# Review the inventory, then delete each exact retired-version cache ID:
gh cache delete <cache-id> --repo tutur3u/platform
```

The search must return no pins. Delete only inventory rows whose keys match
`bun-deps-v1-*-1.4.3-*`; repeat inventory if its limit is reached. Deleting an
already absent ID needs no retry. Do not delete Supabase image keys or add cache
write permissions to PR jobs. Old PR-scoped Gradle/Pods entries will otherwise
age out; source gating does not remove existing archives.

For Linux reproduction, isolate the Supabase project ID and ports, use a
scratch-local Bun matching the repository pin, and remove only that project's
containers and volumes afterward. Supabase CLI 2.117.0 recognizes a missing volume
only by Docker's `no such volume` diagnostic. Docker 29 can instead report
`volume ... not found`, causing fresh startup to skip migrations as if restoring
a backup. A command-scoped `DOCKER_API_VERSION=1.41` restores the expected missing
volume diagnostic on that host. Verify the diagnostic first; do not change the
daemon or global environment. This compatibility issue also reproduces on main
and does not establish the cause of an unrelated CI failure.

### Rust dependency verification

The combined `rust-backend.yml` workflow is paused in `tuturuuu.ci.ts`.
Its disabled switch also applies to manual dispatch; skipped verify jobs do not
prove native or wasm compilation, regardless of the aggregate check result.

`rust-verify.yml` provides a separate manual CI verification route (paused with
Rust). Dispatch it on the ref whose head is the commit to verify and supply that
exact 40-character SHA. The workflow rejects any other SHA, so no dispatch input
selects code to run in a branch's cache scope. It verifies the checkout and records source/workflow SHAs,
manifest and lock hashes, and the Rust toolchain in the run summary. It uses the
repository's Rust 1.95 minimum to run locked native Clippy/tests, wasm Worker
checking and a native release build. It uses read-only repository permissions,
no deployment environment or secrets, and no shared cache writes.

Native tests run before strict Clippy so an unrelated lint failure cannot hide
actual test results for the requested source. Clippy retains `-D warnings` and
still fails the verifier; Worker packaging remains dependent on a successful
verifier. A passing test step alongside failed lint is bounded test evidence,
not a successful Rust gate. Preserve the original failed run and inspect the
exact source and test results separately before resolving review findings.
The ordering and strict-failure policy is covered by
`scripts/ci/rust-verification-workflow.test.js`.

Four private Storage/CMS port modules remain compiled for their regression tests
but deliberately have no dispatcher arms: storage downloads, workspace sharing,
CMS delivery and CMS assets. Their prior direct-download behavior lacks guarded
relay/source parity, so live Next.js retains ownership in `route-overrides.json`.
Only these module declarations carry reasoned `#[expect(dead_code)]`; strict
Clippy stays unchanged and handler source is retained. Crate-level
`deny(unfulfilled_lint_expectations)` rejects an expectation once no diagnostic
fulfills it. Remove the expectation when completing protected parity; the focused
workflow test also rejects reconnecting any of these handlers while its
expectation remains, even if other unused helpers still satisfy that expectation.
Never restore an unsafe dispatcher arm merely to make lint pass.

For dependency drafts, record the requested source SHA and the actual successful
job result. After the existing verifier succeeds, a separate sequential Worker-package job
installs checksum-published stable `worker-build 0.8.7`
with its locked dependencies into runner-temporary storage and runs the actual
release bundler with locked project dependencies and Worker-only features. It
checks the configured legacy `build/worker/shim.mjs` compatibility entry point,
its `build/index.js` target against the configured Wrangler entry, parses the emitted ES modules,
uses isolated pinned Acorn 8.18.0 to follow the default export through aliases
and the vendor Proxy to the same class that owns the emitted `fetch` function.
Selected class/alias bindings must not be reassigned; the check rejects that
unsupported pattern instead of matching an earlier handler to a later class.
It also validates a real WASM function export named `fetch`. It records config/artifact hashes. These are
package contract checks without invoking handlers or proving deployed behavior. The pinned vendor tool selects
wasm-bindgen 0.2.129, wasm-opt 132 and esbuild 0.28.2; this is Worker package
construction, without invoking Wrangler or accessing deploy secrets. The native
job keeps its 45-minute timeout. The sequential bundle job is bounded to 60 minutes,
with 25 minutes for bundler installation and 30 for release bundling; these are
limits, not measured durations. Both steps record elapsed seconds on ordinary command exit, including failures;
use hosted step timestamps if runner cancellation prevents the exit trap.
Record actual hosted duration after the first approved exact-source dispatch;
adjust only with evidence if a bound is insufficient. Docker
container packaging and deployed runtime behavior remain separate evidence gaps. Registering this workflow does not resume
the paused migration/deployment workflow or authorize a production cutover.

### Docker automation

- `docker-setup-check.yaml`
- `rust-backend.yml`

`docker-setup-check.yaml` is the workflow to watch whenever Docker files,
compose files, or Docker helper scripts change. It also watches the manifests
of apps directly represented in the Docker topology and `bun.lock` for
workspace dependency changes. Unrelated app or package version-only bumps do
not rebuild the web images. `rust-backend.yml` owns the
`apps/backend` Rust service checks and the migration Cloudflare checks:
formatting, locked dependency fetch, Clippy, tests, Cloudflare Worker target
validation, smoke reporter unit tests, native binary build, Docker image build,
`apps/tanstack-web` type-check/test validation, and the TanStack route-tree
generator/formatter unit test. Keep `scripts/generate-tanstack-route-tree.*`
in this workflow's path filters so route-tree generation changes run before
TanStack/Rust deployment handoff.

The TanStack/Rust migration is currently paused. Keep `rust-backend.yml`,
`tanstack-route-manifest.yaml`, and
`vercel-production-tanstack-web.yaml` set to `false` in `tuturuuu.ci.ts`; the
shared `ci-check.yml` switchboard will leave the Rust/TanStack jobs skipped.
Re-enable them only when active maintenance resumes and the full workflow is
again an intentional delivery gate.

The shared `e2e-tests.yaml` workflow also keeps `migration-e2e` disabled and
publishes only the `next` image bundle. Maintained Next.js Playwright coverage
continues to run; the retained TanStack dual-stack and comparison matrix is a
manual source reference until migration work resumes.

### Retrying allocated Playwright runs

E2E image bundle tags include the run ID, run attempt, and source SHA. A
failed-jobs-only retry increments the attempt without necessarily rerunning the
successful image preparation job. Shards can then miss that attempt's bundle
and fall back to local image builds, spending their deadline before assertions
finish. After the allocated run's final cleanup succeeds, retry the full workflow
when fresh bundle preparation is needed; never cancel allocated runs, repeatedly
retry blindly, or push over an active allocation to recover a missing bundle.

### E2E runtime budget

The general shard and dedicated invitation runtime commands use GNU `timeout`
against the job's recorded start, allowing up to 37 minutes minus setup
time so eight minutes remain inside the unchanged 45-minute job deadline. Timeout is
an ordinary failed step (exit 124), not a passing or skipped test. TERM is
followed by KILL after 30 seconds if the owned command cannot exit. Existing
failure diagnostics, redaction, artifact upload, and `always()` cleanup still
run; the reserve is a budget, not proof that runner or Docker failures cannot
prevent them. Setup exhausting the runtime budget fails before starting tests.
Validate this policy with `node --test scripts/ci/e2e-runtime-budget.test.js`.

### Lettin E2E fixture and browser diagnostics

The canonical identity/About persistence check uses the same fixed browser phases
and bounded context cleanup as the Markdown/import checks. Each complete phase
has a 60-second cap within the existing 180-second test budget; cleanup retains
the original action/assertion failure even if closing the browser context fails.
Use the last entered profile phase to locate a stalled navigation, banner upload,
save, or reload. A context-close error after the overall timeout is insufficient
to identify the failing profile operation. Coverage is in
`lettin-browser-phase.test.ts` and `lettin-context-cleanup.test.ts`; successful
unit checks do not prove authenticated profile persistence in CI.

Lettin fixture phases print fixed names for account creation, D1 migration and
seeding, browser context/cookie installation, and cleanup. Timed-out owned fixture
subprocesses receive SIGKILL at the existing 60-second deadline so a child ignoring
SIGTERM cannot block Playwright's event loop indefinitely. These diagnostics
identify the last entered phase; an incomplete runner log alone does not prove a
browser, server, or database root cause. Do not include tokens, SQL, account IDs,
response bodies, or authenticated URLs in phase logs.

Lettin workspace GET diagnostics are enabled in CI, or explicitly with
`LETTIN_READ_DIAGNOSTICS=true` for a bounded investigation. They emit fixed
`[lettin-read]` stage names and monotonic elapsed milliseconds for actor resolution,
Cloudflare bindings, D1 reads and Supabase member/permission reads. A started stage
without completion identifies an unfinished dependency; a completed duration shows
where time was spent. Failures preserve the original error while logging only the
stage and elapsed time, never actor/workspace IDs, request URLs, data or raw errors.
These measurements diagnose stalls; they do not change authorization, retries or
request timeouts. Outside CI, leave the flag disabled after collecting evidence.

For wrapped native select controls, Playwright’s exact label matching includes
nested option text. Give the import Source select an explicit localized accessible
label so canonical-file selection remains reliable; the focused import component
test checks the explicit accessible label and associated native labels without
relying on private browser bundles. Maintained authenticated import E2E uses
Playwright’s public `getByLabel('Source', { exact: true })` locator for browser coverage.

The Markdown persistence helper bounds actions at 15 seconds and navigation/reload
at 60 seconds, identifies opening the project dialog separately from navigation,
and uses the same 10-second context-close boundary as canonical imports. Cleanup
errors preserve the original failed assertion. These are diagnostic safeguards,
not proof that a server or runner stall is fixed.

The Markdown persistence helper also logs page creation before navigation,
using the same fixed phase summaries. This exposes a previously silent browser
boundary without claiming it caused the recurring stall. Canonical import
browser checks also emit fixed phase names and use a 15-second action deadline
(the existing 60-second navigation deadline remains). Import context cleanup
has a ten-second bound and retains the original assertion failure if cleanup
also fails; cleanup failure still fails an otherwise successful test. This
prevents a disposed-context error from obscuring the first failed operation.
Regression coverage lives in `lettin-context-cleanup.test.ts`.
Markdown and canonical-import browser phases also use public `test.step` with a
60-second whole-phase cap. Import preview visibility, post-import navigation/content,
and the public privacy response (including its body read) each have an explicit
phase too; they do not sit between capped clicks. It covers the complete awaited phase, including tracing
instrumentation before or after an action; the inner action/navigation/assertion
deadlines and tracing remain unchanged. A phase deadline fails the test and keeps
fixed, safe diagnostics; it never turns the stalled phase into a success or skip.
This contains a possible instrumentation wait and does not prove the cause of a
slow application request or runner shutdown. Regression coverage in
`lettin-browser-phase.test.ts` verifies the public step timeout option and
propagation of a simulated timeout with safe failure diagnostics. This focused
contract test does not launch a browser or prove a stalled browser operation
exits within the deadline; exact-commit E2E remains required.

### E2E runtime heartbeat

For bounded CI stall investigations, the Lettin suite worker and the parent E2E
runner emit a heartbeat every ten seconds with only wall-clock, monotonic-clock,
and process CPU deltas. It is enabled by `CI=true`, or explicitly by
`E2E_RUNTIME_DIAGNOSTICS=true` locally. Worker timers stop after each test; the
parent timer stops when the Playwright command succeeds or fails. Timers are
unreferenced and do not keep either process alive. No identities, fixtures, URLs,
request bodies, or raw errors are included. Timeline page creation, navigation,
and assertions emit fixed operation markers without changing their deadlines.

On Linux, only the parent runner also samples five fixed `/proc` files:
`meminfo`, `vmstat`, and CPU, memory, and I/O pressure. Logs contain only available
memory/free swap in KiB, major fault/swap page counters, cumulative PSI stall
microseconds, and parent RSS bytes. Each asynchronous read allocates at most
32 KiB plus one byte and checks a shared one-second abort signal before and
after I/O. Samples never overlap and suppress late publication after command
cleanup. Unsupported
or unreadable fields emit only `{ unavailable: 1 }`; raw file data and errors
are never logged. These counters can distinguish pressure during delayed ticks;
current readings alone do not prove which process caused it. Regression coverage
in `e2e-runtime-resources.test.js` checks numeric output, privacy, non-overlap,
and stopped publication.

CI shards use the public Playwright JSON discovery receipt to partition selected
tests into sequential cohorts by their declared satellite dependencies. Only a
cohort's owned Next.js dev servers remain live during its tests; launcher process
groups, including descendants, stop before the next cohort starts. Multi-app
invitation cohorts keep their services together. A public Reporter `onBegin`
receipt supplies project dependency metadata omitted by the JSON reporter.
Dependency-connected projects share one invocation so Playwright retains setup
failure and dependent-project skip semantics; independent groups still run.
Selection, including sharding, project filters, and dependencies, happens once;
public `--test-list` manifests execute that selection without repeating setup.
Retries and
assertion deadlines stay unchanged, as does the outer CI runtime budget.

Each successful cohort must report the selected case count and identities; its blob report
is retained for the standard artifact upload and merged JSON acceptance receipt.
Failures remain failures; cleanup failure stops further service startup. Finite
invocation-wide max-failure/global-timeout policies (including configuration),
project repeat runs, explicit no-dependency execution, last-failed/only-changed or unknown selection modes,
unsupported or missing dependency graphs, teardown projects, commands without
an explicit JSON reporter, and single-cohort selections retain the original
single invocation. Malformed discovery receipts fail closed rather than guessing
which services to start. Dependency-connected projects can retain several
satellites until that whole group completes. The default CI shard uses isolation; local runs keep their
existing lifecycle. This trades additional Playwright/global-setup startup and
occasional satellite restarts for releasing accumulated dev-server heaps earlier.
`e2e-satellite-cohorts.test.js` verifies shard/filter/setup coverage through public
Playwright commands, multi-service ownership, merged receipts, and failure cleanup;
`e2e-owned-process-group.test.js` verifies surviving descendant termination. These
focused tests do not establish an exact-commit E2E pass or attribute memory growth
to a particular satellite.

A runner heartbeat continuing while worker ticks stop narrows the problem to the
worker or its output path. Both stopping can also mean host suspension or delayed
log delivery; numeric deltas after recovery help compare those possibilities,
but do not alone establish a root cause. A heartbeat cannot interrupt blocked
JavaScript or guarantee cleanup. Regression coverage in
`e2e-runtime-heartbeat.test.js` verifies numeric-only logs, preserved command and
failure outcomes, and timer cleanup. Exact-commit E2E remains runtime evidence.

### Meet, Lettin, and Parley Cloudflare validation

Meet and Lettin build `@tuturuuu/supabase` before Vitest because proxy tests import
its Node `dist` exports. Meet, Lettin and Parley use `scripts/ci/release-only-changes.js`
to skip PR builds only for version fields, changelogs and release badges; source,
dependencies and missing history still validate. Push/manual behavior is unchanged.
Meet generates build metadata before Turbo/OpenNext: production refs embed
`production`, other refs embed `preview` and the checked-out SHA/ref; these inputs
participate in cache keys. Wrangler descriptions do not populate `/api/build-info`.
Production `scripts/ci/verify-meet-build-info.js` requires HTTP 200, JSON, `appName: meet`,
full candidate SHA and production environment/ref before recording success. Fallback,
stale and preview bundles fail closed; main validation never probes production.
Workflow contracts use Bun's built-in YAML parser via `workflow-yaml-test-helper.js`,
not undeclared transitive YAML packages. The dependency-free snapshot checks ordering,
identity and caching. Run `node --test scripts/ci/meet-build-metadata.test.js scripts/ci/verify-meet-build-info.test.js scripts/ci/generate-build-metadata.test.js`.

Meet, Lettin and Parley pin the official OpenNext `1.20.6` registry tarball as a
shared URL dependency. Its URL-keyed Bun patch backports the Cache Components
scheduler and request-scoped module-loading changes from upstream PR 1318 at
`6b783939aefa8f9a19d4f002f68bc57c62879098`. The older upstream preview rejects Node
middleware; removing that guard does not supply a middleware bundler. Retain the
stable adapter's real `bundleNodeMiddleware` path and apply the Cache Components
middleware patch after that bundle. Preserve component names, preview manifests,
and Next 16.4's `CacheSignal(null)` constructor arguments.

Keep the registry integrity in `bun.lock`; `packages/meet-core` retains its
separate stable-version adapter and patch. Verify installed package isolation
against that independent consumer, not Lettin. Bun's path-based patch command can
select the package version instead of the URL: verify the generated `patchedDependencies` key and restore the
stable patch before installing. Set the URL-keyed entry through `bun pm pkg set`
with JSON input, then verify a frozen install and installed package isolation.
A prepared directory left by `bun patch` can shadow dependency symlinks; preserve
that owned directory outside the resolver and reinstall before testing.

Meet requires both compatibility fixes: the workerd scheduler prevents the
anonymous login render from hanging, and cache-handler registration must return
before Next's original dynamic loader accesses removed minified aliases. Otherwise
even the local-metadata `/api/build-info` handler can fail before it executes.
`scripts/ci/meet-cloudflare-render.runtime.mjs` carries the installed Next
scheduler transformation, cache-handler method and React resume names that the
Meet artifact gates (`scripts/ci/meet-build-metadata.test.js`,
`scripts/ci/verify-meet-start-output.test.js`) require; the former standalone
`meet-cloudflare-render.test.js` no longer exists.
For retained-artifact diagnosis, preserve the original ZIP and hash; normalize
only CI file imports and Wrangler's require shim in a private replay. Use the
canonical URL and Host, local bindings, blocked outbound traffic and bounded
requests. Isolate scheduler and cache-loader changes independently. Such a replay
establishes a mechanism; exact-commit CI builds and hosted health remain separate
delivery gates.

When changing the candidate dependency, update both workflow path filters and
`tuturuuu.ts` selection to its active patch. Selection regressions must derive the
patch from the app manifest and root patchedDependencies rather than an obsolete
filename copied into the test.

Run `node --test apps/parley/scripts/opennext-candidate.test.mjs` for actual installed
Next CJS/ESM AST-patch compatibility and fail-closed source-shape checks. After the
real CI OpenNext build, Parley runs `node --test verify.mjs` from
`apps/parley/test-fixtures/built-worker`. The fixture preserves production compatibility
flags and forwards through the production entry with canonical URL/Host, local assets,
local R2/self bindings and dummy credentials. Global outbound fetch throws; no provider,
production Durable Object or account binding is configured. It requires exact build-info
SHA plus four sequential and four concurrent English/Vietnamese invitation pages,
translated content and complete HTML within bounded deadlines, then closes the harness.
Only hashes and lengths are logged. No release build runs locally. A green fixture
qualifies the anonymous built-page boundary only: authenticated invitation, session,
Live/provider and hosted concurrency acceptance remain required before recovery claims.
Never ship private minified diagnostic patches or infer recovery from HTTP 200 alone.

`parley-offline-diagnostic.yaml` is manual-only from trusted `main`, with no deployment
or production secrets. It replays retained artifact 11583133658 from run 37853687763,
fixed to SHA `387caf4872a59cc4944b16324a2554062393d7d1` and its published archive digest.
Expiry, changed provenance, unsafe extraction or missing Linux tool binaries stop it.
It installs frozen tools without lifecycle scripts, never rebuilds the app, and makes
one anonymous `/access-denied` request inside private mount/network namespaces with
loopback only, local assets/R2/self bindings, dummy credentials and no remote services.
The unit caps aggregate memory/CPU, local state and logs; active work gets 50 seconds
plus 10 seconds for owned process-group cleanup. Missing isolation/caps stop launch.
Only an allowlisted result is retained for one day; request errors or missing HTTP status fail qualification, while a captured HTTP 500 is diagnostic evidence, not health success.
Before retrieval, a finite unit checks memory/CPU/PID caps and private namespaces,
not whole-host boot readiness. Exact digest-bound legacy asset aliases stay inside private extraction without changing ZIP/JS bytes; offline gaps never allow online fallback.

### TanStack/Rust Cloudflare deployment

`rust-backend.yml` is also the manually dispatched Cloudflare preview deployment
workflow for the migration pair:

- Rust backend Worker: `apps/backend/wrangler.jsonc`, Worker name
  `tuturuuu-backend`.
- TanStack Start Worker: `apps/tanstack-web/wrangler.jsonc`, Worker name
  `tuturuuu-tanstack-web`.

The workflow stays switchboard-controlled by the `rust-backend.yml` entry in
`tuturuuu.ts`, which is currently disabled while the migration is paused. Pull
request and push runs are validation-only and use
`contents: read`; they do not require Cloudflare secrets just to type-check,
test, lint config, build the Rust Worker bundle, or build the backend Docker
image.

Manual dispatch inputs:

- `deploy_target`: `none`, `backend`, `tanstack-web`, or `all`.
- `deployment_mode`: `dry-run` or `deploy`. Keep the default `dry-run` for the
  first run in a new account or environment.

Run `rust-backend.yml` from `main` for Cloudflare deployments. The deployment
preflight requires the dispatch ref to be `refs/heads/main` and `github.actor`
to be listed in the comma-delimited `TRUSTED_CLOUDFLARE_DEPLOY_ACTORS`
repository variable before it loads `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`. Keep that allowlist
limited to maintainers who can approve secret-backed Worker deployments.
Cloudflare deploy credentials must not be exposed to arbitrary branch code;
review or merge deployment changes before dispatching a secret-backed run.

The deploy jobs are bound to the `cloudflare-workers-preview` GitHub
Environment. Configure these GitHub values there before expecting deployment
jobs to run:

| Name                                      | GitHub storage       | Purpose                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`                    | Environment secret   | Cloudflare API token with Workers Scripts edit access for this account.                             |
| `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`                   | Environment variable | Cloudflare account id used by Wrangler. A same-named secret is accepted only as a fallback.         |
| `BACKEND_WORKER_ORIGIN`                   | Environment variable | Deployed Rust backend Worker origin used by the post-deploy smoke gate.                             |
| `TANSTACK_WEB_WORKER_ORIGIN`              | Environment variable | Deployed TanStack Worker origin used by the post-deploy smoke gate.                                 |
| `CLOUDFLARE_SMOKE_BACKEND_INTERNAL_TOKEN` | Environment secret   | Dedicated smoke token mapped to `BACKEND_INTERNAL_TOKEN` only while running `bun smoke:cloudflare`. |

If either value is missing, the workflow emits a
`Cloudflare deployment skipped` warning, records setup guidance in the job
summary, and skips deploy jobs after CI validation has completed. The warning
names only the missing GitHub Environment keys, not their values. A non-empty
but invalid or under-scoped token normally surfaces as a Worker secret preflight
skip or a Wrangler failure before upload.

Worker runtime secrets live in Cloudflare, not GitHub. After the GitHub
credential preflight passes, a dedicated Worker secret preflight checks the
selected Workers with `wrangler secret list`.
It reads only secret names, never secret values. If Wrangler cannot list names,
or if any required name is
missing, the workflow emits a warning, writes setup commands to the job summary,
and skips the selected deploy job instead of failing later inside a deploy
step. Missing-secret warnings use the `Missing Worker secrets` wording and list
only secret names plus `bun wrangler secret put ...` commands; they never print
or infer secret values.

| Worker                  | Required Cloudflare Worker secrets                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tuturuuu-backend`      | `BACKEND_INTERNAL_TOKEN`, `TUTURUUU_APP_COORDINATION_SECRET`, `SUPABASE_URL`, `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`, `CRON_SECRET`, `DISCORD_APP_DEPLOYMENT_URL`, `AURORA_EXTERNAL_URL`, `AURORA_EXTERNAL_WSID` |
| `tuturuuu-tanstack-web` | `BACKEND_PUBLIC_ORIGIN`, `BACKEND_INTERNAL_TOKEN`                                                                                                                                                     |

Bootstrap missing Worker secrets from a trusted local shell with Wrangler:

```sh
bun wrangler secret put BACKEND_INTERNAL_TOKEN --config apps/backend/wrangler.jsonc
bun wrangler secret put TUTURUUU_APP_COORDINATION_SECRET --config apps/backend/wrangler.jsonc
bun wrangler secret put SUPABASE_URL --config apps/backend/wrangler.jsonc
bun wrangler secret put SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY --config apps/backend/wrangler.jsonc
bun wrangler secret put CRON_SECRET --config apps/backend/wrangler.jsonc
bun wrangler secret put DISCORD_APP_DEPLOYMENT_URL --config apps/backend/wrangler.jsonc
bun wrangler secret put AURORA_EXTERNAL_URL --config apps/backend/wrangler.jsonc
bun wrangler secret put AURORA_EXTERNAL_WSID --config apps/backend/wrangler.jsonc
bun wrangler secret put BACKEND_PUBLIC_ORIGIN --config apps/tanstack-web/wrangler.jsonc
bun wrangler secret put BACKEND_INTERNAL_TOKEN --config apps/tanstack-web/wrangler.jsonc
```

Deploy the backend before the TanStack Worker when `deploy_target` is not `all`.
The TanStack Worker has a `BACKEND` service binding to `tuturuuu-backend`, so a
frontend-only deployment assumes the backend Worker and its secrets already
exist. When `deploy_target=all`, a skipped backend deployment also keeps the
TanStack deployment skipped, even if the TanStack Worker secrets are present.

`deployment_mode=dry-run` compiles and runs Wrangler checks without uploading,
but it still uses the same Cloudflare account, token, Worker name, and secret
name preflights as `deployment_mode=deploy`. Treat a dry-run skip as a setup
gap, not as a deploy failure. `deployment_mode=deploy` uploads the selected
Worker version only after those preflights pass.

When `deploy_target=all` and `deployment_mode=deploy`, the
`post-deploy-smoke` job runs only after both Worker deploy jobs succeed. It
requires `BACKEND_WORKER_ORIGIN`, `TANSTACK_WEB_WORKER_ORIGIN`, and
`CLOUDFLARE_SMOKE_BACKEND_INTERNAL_TOKEN`; missing values fail the full deploy
workflow with a warning, an error, and setup guidance in the step summary
instead of silently skipping runtime verification. The warning title is
`Cloudflare smoke inputs missing`, and the error title is
`Cloudflare smoke verification blocked`. The job runs:

```sh
bun smoke:cloudflare --output "$CLOUDFLARE_SMOKE_REPORT_PATH"
```

The JSON report is written under
`tmp/benchmarks/web-migration/<run-id>-<attempt>/cloudflare-smoke.json`,
uploaded as the `cloudflare-smoke-<run-id>-<attempt>` workflow artifact, and
summarized in the GitHub step summary. The report must come from the deployed
backend and TanStack Worker origins; do not point these variables at local
Wrangler or Docker origins in the `cloudflare-workers-preview` Environment.

### Quality and security

- `type-check.yaml`
- `turbo-unit-tests.yaml`
- `biome-check.yaml`
- `codeql.yml`
- `security-checks.yaml`
- `security-review-classifier.yaml`
- `security-review-recheck.yaml` (permissionless review signal)
- `security-review-reclassify.yaml` (default-branch recompute after reviews)
- `security-review-sweep.yaml` (hourly default-branch recompute of one 1/24 partition of open PRs; revocation backstop)
- `codecov.yaml`
- `i18n-check.yaml`
- `check-migrations.yml`
- `check-migration-timestamps.yml`
- `branch-name-check.yaml`

The test workflows (`turbo-unit-tests.yaml` and `codecov.yaml`) run `bun setup`
through `scripts/ci/run-with-backoff.sh` before executing tests so dependency
installation and workspace package builds match the local setup path while
surviving transient tarball extraction failures. The Codecov coverage test run
also uses the helper with a two-attempt cap so transient runner interruptions
such as exit code `130` retry once without masking deterministic test failures.
Vercel workflows should invoke Turborepo through `bun turbo:local ...` after the
retried `bun install` so CI uses the pinned repo dependency instead of resolving
a global or downloaded Turbo binary. Cacheable builds, type checks, and tests
must be executed through `.github/actions/run-with-turbo-remote-cache`; trusted
jobs pass the dedicated repository `TURBO_TOKEN` and `TURBO_TEAM` variable,
while pull-request and Dependabot jobs leave both inputs empty and use the
task-family local fallback cache.

The secretless fallback archives only `.turbo/cache` under v2 keys partitioned
by OS, architecture, task family, Turbo configuration hash, lockfile hash, and
commit. Restoration tries the exact key, then the same-lock prefix. Only
`type-check.yaml` opts into a final same-config prefix across lock generations.
Turbo still validates each task hash and both dependency builds and type checks
run; a changed lockfile can invalidate every task even after archive restoration.
Only non-PR, non-Dependabot jobs on the repository default branch save archives.
Feature, production, PR, and Dependabot runs remain restore-only, with GitHub's
branch cache scope preventing main from restoring feature-produced entries.
The protected remote-token expressions remain unchanged: this does not enable
feature-branch Turbo Remote Cache.

The action exposes `cache-hit` (exact-key match) and `cache-matched-key` (empty on
miss). Its job summary distinguishes archive MISS, exact restore, and prefix
restore from actual Turbo task hits. Inspect each command's Cached/Tasks totals
before claiming reuse. A successful default-branch run must seed a new v2 archive;
deleted archives cannot be recovered by broader prefixes. Before claiming a
speedup, record the exact CI SHA, archive size, matched key, per-task hits, and
elapsed time; archive download cost and retention can outweigh reuse.
Regression coverage: `node --test .github/actions/setup-turbo-fallback-cache/action.test.js`.

Vercel deploy credentials must stay environment-scoped. Do not put
`${{ secrets.* }}` values in a Vercel workflow-level `env:` block, and do not
export production Supabase, encryption, or provider secrets from GitHub
Actions. Store app runtime and build-time configuration in the Vercel project
environment. Remote-cache identity is the narrow exception: it is passed only
to the wrapped `vercel build` step and never written to `GITHUB_ENV` or a
workflow/job environment. The regression test
`bun test scripts/ci/release-workflows.test.js` enforces this for every
`vercel-preview-*.yaml` and `vercel-production-*.yaml` workflow.

### Cache and artifact resources

`actions-storage-report.yaml` runs weekly and can be dispatched manually. It
is read-only: it queries the repository's live Actions cache policy and current
cache/artifact inventories, groups cache bytes by key prefix, and summarizes
artifact count, size, age, and largest workflow families. Cache status is
informational at 80% of the configured limit, warning at 90%, and critical at
100%. The report does not assume a fixed artifact byte entitlement and does not
require an organization billing token.

The July 10, 2026 audit found a 10 GB cache maximum and 7-day retention. Target
steady-state usage below 9 GB so GitHub does not continuously evict and recreate
high-reuse entries. Prefer Bun downloads, package-manager data, task-family
Turbo state, native dependencies, shared Rust state, and service-scoped
BuildKit layers over final application binaries. Leave managed uv and CodeQL
caching to their official actions.

All `upload-artifact` steps must set `retention-days` and
`if-no-files-found`. Optional failure diagnostics may warn; release and deploy
handoffs must fail when absent. E2E diagnostics are failure-only and retained 7
days, package tarballs are retained 1 day, development mobile deliverables 7
days, and production store deliverables 14 days.

Preview deploy credentials must not be exposed to arbitrary branch push code.
Most preview Vercel workflows are manual-only: run the workflow from `main`,
provide the branch, tag, or SHA in `preview_ref`, and keep
`TRUSTED_PREVIEW_DEPLOY_ACTORS` limited to maintainers who can approve
secret-backed preview builds. The workflow still checks out and builds the
requested `preview_ref`, so reviewers should treat that ref as code that can
execute during install/build.

CodeQL runs from the repository-owned `codeql.yml` (GitHub default setup is not
configured; do not enable both). It scans pull requests and `main` pushes for the
languages the diff touches, and `security-checks.yaml` runs it daily. Neither
workflow calls the `ci-check` switchboard: its selectors run from the PR checkout,
so the scope jobs read their selectors from the base commit instead. Pull requests
fail only on new high/critical results; `bun git-sync` mirrors the already-scanned
`main` commit to `production`. See [Security review cadence](/build/devops/security-cadence).

`scripts/ci/codeql-new-alerts.js` is the trusted new-alert gate for a
repository-owned pull request CodeQL workflow. That workflow reads it from the
pull request's base commit (`HEAD^1` of the merge ref, so never from pull
request code). It fails only on high/critical results that are absent from
`main`'s latest analysis of the same category. It pages through `main`'s
analyses within a fixed bound to find that baseline. A category with no `main`
analysis fails closed, as does a rule whose severity is unknown or unreadable.
The public log carries counts only; triage results by alert number in the
maintainer-only Security tab. A category such as `/language:actions` needs a
`main` analysis, from default setup or a trusted `main` run, before pull
requests can pass on pre-existing findings.

`scripts/ci/security-scan-diff.js` is the matching trusted differ for the
repository-owned dependency audit and secret scan. They load it from the base
commit as well. A pull request fails only on high/critical advisories absent
at the base commit, and the public log shows counts by severity. Pre-existing
advisories are tracked in the findings register, not on unrelated pull
requests.

E2E suites reuse only exact same-day success proofs from protected `main`.
See [E2E proof reuse](/build/devops/e2e-proof-reuse) for suite inputs, conservative
fallbacks, diagnostics safety, and inactive database proposal handling.

`docker-setup-check.yaml`, `turbo-unit-tests.yaml`, `codecov.yaml`, and
`type-check.yaml` use the same gate before their expensive jobs, so version-only
package manifest edits do not rebuild images or repeat unchanged tests and type
checks. Manual dispatch remains a full run.

Supabase migration workflows still consume the required platform workflow-run
signals, but compare the target SHA with the last successful migration marker.
Only database and migration-control changes proceed to Supabase CLI setup and
`db push`; an unavailable marker fails open. Staging and production each use a
single serialized evaluate-and-migrate job, and production preserves the
same-SHA platform deployment plus staging-success prerequisites.

Cloudflare Worker manual deployments follow the same trust boundary: run
`rust-backend.yml` from `main`, keep `TRUSTED_CLOUDFLARE_DEPLOY_ACTORS` limited
to trusted maintainers, and avoid exposing `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` to unreviewed
branch code. The workflow checks the protected dispatch ref and actor allowlist
before loading Cloudflare credentials or running Worker deploy steps.

`vercel-preview-platform.yaml` also runs on protected `main` pushes. Keep that
exception narrow: `supabase-staging.yaml` is triggered by the platform preview
build workflow and production migration requires a successful `main` staging
migration for the same SHA before it can run `supabase db push --include-all`.

### Other delivery surfaces

- `discord-modal-deploy.yml`
- `mobile-build-android.yaml`
- `mobile-build-ios.yaml`
- `mobile-build-macos.yaml`
- `mobile-build-windows.yaml`
