## Operational Rules

### Manual dispatch

Use `workflow_dispatch` when:

- you need to rerun a deployment intentionally
- you need to promote a migration outside the normal trigger timing
- you need to recover from a failed but otherwise understood automation path

Manual dispatch bypasses affected-app gating. Generic switchboard-controlled
workflows still honor disabled `ci` entries, while trusted manual satellite
preview workflows launch their guarded deploy job directly and do not keep an
unused `tuturuuu.ts` toggle.

For preview Vercel deployments, dispatch the workflow from `main`, set
`preview_ref` to the branch, tag, or SHA to deploy, and confirm the actor is in
`TRUSTED_PREVIEW_DEPLOY_ACTORS`. Do not reintroduce preview `push` triggers for
secret-backed Vercel workflows, and do not add a standalone `check-ci` job to a
manual-only preview: the dispatch already selected the build and the extra job
only consumes another runner. Preview concurrency uses the workflow plus
`preview_ref`, so rerunning the same target cancels stale work without canceling
a different preview target.

Package release workflows that expose production secrets or trusted publishing
authority must add their own ref guard before dependency installation or publish
jobs. Release Please is the only workflow that generates monorepo version and
changelog PRs. It runs from `production`, uses
`secrets.RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN` so generated PRs and releases can trigger
downstream workflows, and falls back to `github.token` only to keep the job from
failing when the bot token is not provisioned. The `github.token` fallback does
not trigger downstream workflow runs from generated release PRs. Release Please
rejects non-production manual dispatches before the write-capable release job.
`release-please-transient-retry.yaml` retries only the GitHub API disconnect
reported as `release-please failed: other side closed`. It checks that the run
is still failed on the current production SHA, then reruns failed jobs for at
most three total attempts. Other failures remain visible for investigation;
a manual rerun supersedes a queued automatic retry.
Generated release-note normalization preserves published history and unrelated
feature descriptions. The offline checkout entry from #5734 is a narrow exception:
when both its original commit and merge commit appear in the same unpublished
section, the normalizer retains one description that includes cached images and
all references. Both exact commit identities and titles must match; similar
wording or a lone commit never enables this consolidation. Regression coverage is
in `scripts/ci/normalize-release-notes.test.js`. Regenerate through the maintained
production Release Please workflow after promoting a generator fix; do not edit
generated changelogs or version fields manually.

Package publish workflows consume release-please version bumps on `production`;
they must not recreate checksum or PR-title version bump automation. Package
release workflows use npm trusted publishing: build and artifact-pack work runs
before any OIDC permission is granted, then the `publish-npm` job downloads one
tarball, verifies its package name and version, and runs `npm publish` without
`NPM_TOKEN`. Each publish job is bound to its package release environment, and
the matching npm trusted publisher must use this repository, the workflow
filename, and that environment. Manual dispatch is only valid with the branch
selector set to `production`; non-production refs are rejected before the package
or publish jobs can start. Every workflow-published package manifest must also
declare `repository.type: "git"`,
`repository.url: "https://github.com/tutur3u/platform"`, and
`repository.directory` matching the package path. npm validates those fields
against GitHub Actions provenance and rejects publishes with `E422` when the
packed manifest has an empty or mismatched repository URL. The tarball handoff
uses required-file behavior, one-day retention, and compression level 0 because
`.tgz` is already compressed. Preparation runs any package lifecycle build
through root Turbo first, then calls `npm pack --ignore-scripts` so `prepack`
cannot bypass the shared cache wrapper.

The SDK build embeds only its reviewed portable HTTP-client and task-codec source
closure from the broad `internal-api` and `utils` packages. Those packages remain
development dependencies; emitted JavaScript and declarations share rewritten local
`dist/_portable` imports. `dist/portable-sources.json` records included source paths.
The build rejects unreviewed modules, private/runtime-specific imports, and
undeclared external libraries. Extend the explicit allowlists only after reviewing
the added closure. Keep the isolated public npm install and compiled CLI probes as
the acceptance gate; source-staging tests do not establish package delivery.
Run `node --test packages/sdk/scripts/portable-build.test.cjs` for the boundary
regressions, and require exact-commit compilation and install qualification in CI.

SDK qualification has two explicit phases. Only same-repository pull requests from
`release-please--branches--production` into `production` select SOURCE. That phase
keeps the serial exact-head compile, portable closure/resource controls, manifest
rewrite and archive inventory/integrity checks. Its receipt has `phase: source`,
`sourceValidated: true` and `qualified: false`: it is source readiness, never public
package acceptance. Ordinary PRs and manual qualification retain the full PUBLIC
phase. This avoids requiring unpublished generated dependency versions before the
release can reach the production-only publishers.

After the existing bounded upstream package readiness gate, SDK production
preparation runs PUBLIC qualification against the exact production SHA: exact
public registry tuples, isolated npm consumer installation and compiled CLI/resource
probes. Runtime, peer and optional workspace dependencies must be publicly available;
embedded development-only dependencies are excluded from registry prerequisites.
Missing dependencies fail closed, including optional dependencies that npm might
otherwise omit. Resolve physical dependency manifests from the installed SDK's
Node module search paths inside the disposable consumer. npm may place a direct
dependency under `node_modules/tuturuuu/node_modules` rather than hoist it to the
consumer root. Match the lock entry for that exact physical directory; use the
same verified entry for registry tuple comparison. Reject symlinks in every path
component, missing packages, manifest identity/version mismatches, linked lock
entries and missing or invalid public registry integrity. An invalid nested copy
must not fall back to a valid hoisted copy. The focused
`scripts/ci/sdk-installed-dependencies.test.js` suite covers these layouts and
failure boundaries without installing packages or evaluating their code.
The preparation uploads the very tarball installed and probed,
along with its receipt. The OIDC job requires a successful PUBLIC receipt for the
same SHA, package name/version and SHA256 bytes before publishing that tarball.
No rebuild or second pack follows qualification. No receipt, a SOURCE receipt,
failed cleanup, changed SHA or changed tarball blocks publication. The existing
bounded publisher defer/dispatch protocol remains the resume mechanism for missing
upstream versions; do not manually publish prospective release versions.

Run `node --test scripts/ci/qualify-sdk-package.test.js scripts/ci/package-release-readiness.test.js packages/sdk/scripts/portable-build.test.cjs`
for phase, cycle, runtime dependency, artifact binding and portable closure controls.
These injected non-build controls do not replace exact-SHA hosted compilation and
public-consumer acceptance. Release integration and production promotion retain
separate owner approval and exact-commit CI gates.

SDK packed-CLI qualification keeps install failure stream byte counts and SHA256
commitments, without retaining stdout/stderr or the private npm cache. Its receipt
also extracts at most eight package requests from strict npm E404 lines in the
first 4096 bytes of each stream. Only the HTTPS npm public registry origin and
validated package names are allowed; an exact version is included only when a
matching npm package/version line exists. Credentialed URLs, query strings,
fragments, other registries and free-form errors are excluded. A missing identity
or null version remains unknown; a request is not proof the package exists.
Run `node --test scripts/ci/qualify-sdk-package.test.js` for the diagnostic and
fixture-cleanup regressions. Use the exact-head qualification receipt for new
failures; hashes from older receipts cannot recover discarded npm output.

SDK qualification concurrency identifies PRs by the positive PR number in the
event payload, preserving per-PR supersession and independent rerun/manual groups.
Its workflow remains limited to raw-head PR and manual qualification; keep the
forbidden-trigger, secret, token-permission and publication assertions in
`scripts/ci/qualify-sdk-package.test.js` intact when changing shared CI policy.

Test, Coverage, Biome, and Type Check supersede older main validation runs.
Production and generated Release Please refs retain immutable concurrency groups.
A rapid generated branch reset followed by its metadata commit must not cancel
checks for a SHA also used by main or production. Ordinary feature refs retain
branch push supersession; manual validation attempts remain independent. Cancellation is not a
successful validation or a valid duplicate skip. Resource-owning E2E and database
workflows retain their own lifecycle policies.

The duplicate-proof runner job is scheduled only for generated Release Please
branch pushes. Ordinary feature, main, production and manual runs proceed directly
from preflight to validation, avoiding three extra runner allocations and checkout/
Node setup stages across Test, Coverage and Biome. A skipped proof job is not a
validation receipt; downstream gates still require the actual checks.
Regression coverage: `scripts/ci/generated-proof-scheduling.test.js` executes the
real workflow conditions, including skipped/failed proof and successful reuse.

Generated duplicate pushes can cleanly skip these three workflows' validation
jobs only after `scripts/ci/check-completed-validation.js` proves a completed
successful main or production push at the exact same SHA. It selects the newest
run per canonical branch from complete history, including pending and failed
runs; a newer non-success run vetoes older success. Test and Coverage
require all four successful shard jobs and their successful aggregate. Biome
requires both successful format and lint jobs. The helper checks the current run
attempt again after reading its jobs. Pending, cancelled, skipped, neutral,
partial, failed, or inaccessible proof never substitutes for validation; checks
run normally when proof is unavailable. A failed proof job (including checkout or
Node setup failure) or missing output also runs validation; dependent gates
bypass the implicit success guard and skip only for a successful proof job with
explicit `run_checks=false`. Cancellation and shared CI configuration/release
relevance decisions still apply. Main and production always validate
independently. This changes future runs only and does not rewrite historical
cancelled checks attached to a shared SHA.

Biome retains automatic validation on generated release and overflow-notes
branches plus manual dispatch. The CI switchboard checks committed overflow
content before expensive work, and completed exact-commit duplicate proof can
skip validation without creating cancelled checks. Keep generated mutation and
report guards: skipped or cancelled lint/format jobs must not publish a success
report or open a format follow-up. When verifying a release, inspect all check
runs for its SHA as well as branch-filtered workflow runs. Proof queries share a
45-second overall deadline and fail open to normal validation on timeout.

Release Please can move an oversized generated pull request body into
`release-notes.md` on a companion
`release-please--branches--<branch>--release-notes` branch. The workflow runs
`node scripts/ci/release-please-overflow-recovery.js --target-branch production`
before `googleapis/release-please-action@v5`; when a merged pending release PR
still points at a missing overflow file, the script recreates the branch and
file from the merged manifest bump and current `production` changelogs, then the
normal Release Please action can create the releases. Missing companion refs are
published only after their notes blob, tree, and final commit exist: recovery
never first creates a ref at the production SHA. This prevents a second notes
push from cancelling duplicate checks on the production commit.

Release Please's own overflow rewrite is not atomic: it resets the notes branch
to the target branch, then commits `release-notes.md`. If it fails in between,
the still-open release PR points at a missing file and every later run fails
with `Failed to find file: release-notes.md` while parsing that PR, freezing the
release PR and its checks on a stale head. When no merged pending PR needs
recovery, the script therefore also restores the notes of an open overflow
release PR, reading its changelog entries from the PR head.

For the exact production overflow-notes ref, CI verifies the committed delta
against production history with `scripts/ci/overflow-notes-ci.js`. An ancestor
bootstrap with no new work, or a generated notes-only addition/change, skips
heavy downstream jobs through the shared preflight; the inline type-check and
E2E preflight use the same predicate. Source changes, malformed notes, missing
history, ordinary generated release PRs, manual events, main, and production
retain normal validation. Notes refs cannot supersede their own coverage, unit,
E2E, Biome, or baseline runs before this decision. A successful preflight with
skipped downstream jobs means no compilation or runtime validation occurred.
Historical cancelled job conclusions cannot be changed by this fix.

Generated production overflow-notes validation uses a commit-specific concurrency
group. Disabling active-run cancellation alone still lets GitHub replace a pending
run in a shared group; a separate notes group for each SHA preserves the validated
skip result for rapid generated updates. Other branches keep their existing groups.

Regression coverage: `overflow-notes-ci.test.js` and
`release-please-overflow-recovery.test.js` cover committed source/content
boundaries and final-ref publication ordering. If the script reports
`skipped`, inspect the pending labels and merged release PR body before retrying.

The same workflow then runs
`node scripts/ci/release-please-auto-approve.js --target-branch production`,
which approves the generated release PR while it is still nothing but generated
output. The `Protected branches` ruleset requires an approving review, so an
untouched release PR otherwise sits at `REVIEW_REQUIRED` indefinitely. Every one
of these must hold or the script skips and leaves the PR for a human: the head
branch is a `release-please--branches--` branch against the target branch, the
PR was opened by a release automation identity, every commit is a
`chore(release): release ...` commit by that same account, and every changed
file is one release-please itself rewrites. That last allowlist is **derived
from `release-please-config.json`** — each package's changelog, its version file
for its release type, and its `extra-files` — so adding a package or changing
its release type cannot silently widen what auto-approval accepts.

Nothing needs to un-approve: the ruleset sets `dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push`,
so any later push to the release branch drops the approval, including one this
workflow never observes. The step deliberately uses `github.token` rather than
`RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN`, because GitHub refuses a review from the account that
opened the pull request — release-please and the approval have to be different
identities. While `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN` is unset both are `github-actions[bot]`,
and the script reports `blocked` and leaves the run green rather than failing.
Use `--dry-run` to see the decision without posting a review.

Generated release formatting also refreshes Bun workspace-version metadata with
pinned Bun 1.4.4 using `--lockfile-only --ignore-scripts`. The shared
`release-workspace-lock.js` validator accepts only workspace `version` string
changes matching the generated package manifests. It rejects dependency,
resolution, workspace identity, root version and unrelated formatting changes;
every other lockfile byte must remain identical. Auto-approval independently
loads complete lock/package files at immutable base/head SHAs and reruns that
validation; `bun.lock` is never an unconditional generated-path exception.
The working-tree guard includes nonignored untracked files and rejects authored
spill without staging it. For files above the [Contents API inline-body limit](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/contents#get-repository-content),
approval reads object metadata at the immutable commit/path and retrieves the
matching [Git blob](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/git/blobs#get-a-blob) through
the same repository API. It ignores response-provided download URLs, caps file
size at 16 MiB, and verifies complete canonical base64, byte size, Git blob SHA
and UTF-8 before validating the lock. Missing or mismatched bodies fail closed.
Run this refresh and the merge helper in CI; the merge helper invokes broad
checks and must not run on agent machines where local builds are prohibited.
Formatting amends the original release commit without resetting its author and
pushes with an exact lease. Approval is pinned to the validated head. If refs
move or validation fails, regenerate/review the release instead of publishing
an ordinary authored repair commit. Published notes stay unchanged; ancestry
alone does not prove differently worded features are duplicates.

`release-please-auto-merge.yaml` closes the loop on the generated release PR. It
runs daily at 00:00 UTC (`cron: "0 0 * * *"`), which is 07:00 in Vietnam
(UTC+7), and on manual dispatch. It does not reimplement the merge in YAML: it
runs `bun git-release-please` and then `bun git-sync`, the same two commands the
release flow uses locally, so the scheduled path and the manual path cannot
drift. Those scripts own the merge rules — platform version sync, conflict
detection, `bun validate`, and fast-forward safety — and are covered by
`scripts/git-release-please.test.js` and `scripts/git-sync.test.js`.

The generated PR must have passing checks, no unresolved active review threads,
and a 5-minute quiet period after its latest update or generated commit. This
is checked before dependency setup and again immediately before merging the
pinned generated head. Failed PR checks stop the daily run for investigation.
After local validation, it pushes the release merge to `main` and waits for all
other workflows on that exact SHA to finish successfully. A failed, missing, or
unfinished check blocks production. The waiter observes the same green run set
twice and rejects a changed main head. Production sync uses
`bun git-sync --current-branch --only-branch production`, pinning the validated
commit instead of silently adopting newer work. The run summary distinguishes
planned work, a completed local merge, dry runs, and completed promotion.

Both initial validation and advanced-main retries derive their build filters from
`package.json`'s canonical `setup` script through `scripts/ci/build-release-setup.mjs`.
The helper parses arguments without executing setup shell text, and both paths
use the same step-scoped Turbo remote-cache wrapper.

If another PR lands on `main` during release validation, the push step fetches
and merges the new head, reinstalls its frozen dependency graph and rebuilds the
dist-only setup packages before rerunning `bun validate`. Affected mobile changes
also refresh `flutter pub get` before mobile checks. The push retries up to four
times. An install or setup failure stops the retry; checks must never validate a
new source commit against dependencies installed for an older checkout. A merge conflict or a push error unrelated to
main advancing fails the run. The exact-SHA CI gate still runs after the push.

Validation runs at two Turbo tasks and two Vitest workers, with the worker limit
preserved through Turbo's strict environment. SDK resource-admission tests start
real child processes and use bounded integration-test deadlines, rather than the
five-second unit-test default that repeatedly failed on hosted runners. These
limits retain the serialization, nested-command, cancellation, and surviving-child
assertions; they do not skip tests or retry a failed merge blindly.

The workflow resolves what to do before it installs anything. It prefers
`origin/release-please--branches--production`, ignores the companion
`--release-notes` overflow branch, and skips the merge entirely when the release
branch is already an ancestor of `origin/main` — so a run with nothing to merge
is a clean no-op rather than a red run. It separately checks whether
`origin/production` has drifted from `origin/main` and syncs even when there was
no merge, which is what makes the schedule self-healing. Every run that pushes
ends by asserting the two refs resolve to the same commit and fails loudly if
they do not.

An empty daily run remains harmless because the workflow exits cleanly when
there is no generated release branch to merge and the protected branches are
already aligned.

The job checks out `main` with `fetch-depth: 0` and
`secrets.RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN`, falling back to `github.token`. The fallback
cannot complete a release: the `Protected branches` ruleset covers `main` and
`production` and its only bypass actor is `OrganizationAdmin`, so a run on
`github.token` merges cleanly and then dies on
`GH013: Changes must be made through a pull request`. `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN`
must therefore hold a fine-grained personal access token for this repository
(Contents, Pull requests, Issues and Workflows read/write; Actions and Commit
statuses read) owned by an organization admin. It is an environment secret of `release-please`
(branches `main` and `production`, admin bypass off), which both
`release-please.yaml` and this job declare, so a workflow on any other branch
cannot read it. Granting the Actions app a ruleset bypass is **not**
an alternative: pushes made with `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not trigger `push`
workflows, so the `production` push would silently skip
`Production Deployment Planner` and the next `Release Please` run and
stall the release chain. A run that would need to push checks for the secret up
front and fails with an actionable error, rather than discovering it after
`bun validate`. Read-only gates (release PR readiness and exact-main CI waits) use the job's
`github.token` with `checks: read` and `statuses: read`: a fine-grained PAT
cannot be granted the Checks permission, so it cannot see check runs.

The job also installs Flutter (`3.47.x`, the same pin as `mobile.yaml`) and runs
`flutter pub get` in `apps/mobile` before the merge. When a release includes
mobile changes, `touchesMobile()` in `scripts/git-release-please.js` follows
`bun validate` with `bun check:mobile`; without a toolchain `dart-format`,
`flutter-analyze` and `flutter-test` all exit `127`.

Keep every mobile build/deploy workflow on that same Flutter minor. The mobile
lockfile is resolved with Dart 3.13; Flutter 3.44.9 bundles Dart 3.12.2 and
downgrades 16 locked packages during `flutter pub get`, which dirties the
checkout before `bun git-release-please` can begin.

Top-level `permissions` is `{}` and
`contents: write` is granted on the job alone, and `concurrency` is grouped with
`cancel-in-progress: false` because cancelling a half-finished release merge
would leave `main` and `production` split. Use the `dry_run` dispatch input to
exercise the merge and run `bun git-sync --no-push` without publishing anything.

Keep internal Tuturuuu dependencies as `workspace:*` in source package
manifests so local builds always use the checked-out workspace. Package release
workflows must first run
`node scripts/ci/package-release-readiness.js gate-package-release packages/<name>`
in a short pre-build gate. The gate checks the package version and publishable
Tuturuuu workspace dependencies once, dispatches missing dependency workflows,
and exits green without build, pack, or publish work while dependencies are
pending. If a dependency workflow for the same production SHA already failed,
completed successfully without npm visibility, or cannot be inspected, the gate
fails immediately. When the gate outputs `should_publish == true` and
`dependencies_ready == true`, the workflow can build and rewrite the checked-out
manifest immediately before `npm pack` with
`node scripts/ci/prepare-npm-package-manifest.js packages/<name>`. That
temporary rewrite replaces `workspace:` protocol ranges with the current
workspace package versions so npm consumers can install the tarball. It must
preserve package-included `file:` tarball dependencies, such as `@tuturuuu/ui`'s
vendored SheetJS tarball, instead of rewriting them to mutable external tarball
URLs. After
`npm publish`, the publish job polls `npm view` for the exact published version
before it reports success, then a separate non-OIDC job dispatches direct
dependent package workflows without checking out the repo or carrying publish
authority. The internal
`node scripts/ci/package-release-readiness.js dispatch-dependent-workflows packages/<name>`
command is available for direct/manual dispatches that can read the checkout.
If npm returns first-publish or permission errors, fix the npm package access and
trusted publisher setup instead of skipping the package. If a published package
depends on another release-please-managed Tuturuuu package, that dependency also
needs its own
`release-*-package.yaml` workflow and matching `tuturuuu.ts` entry.

The platform production Vercel workflow also runs
`node scripts/ci/package-release-readiness.js gate-changed-package-versions`
before installing dependencies. Release-please package bumps therefore publish
and become visible on npm before the normal production platform deployment
continues. The helper intentionally checks only the checked-out latest commit,
not the whole push event payload, so package changes from earlier commits in a
multi-commit push are not bound to an unrelated newer SHA. If the latest commit
does change package manifests, the deploy job grants `actions: write` because
the helper may dispatch missing package release workflows for that same
production SHA. When related package releases are queued or running, the helper
sets `packages_ready=false`; the platform build skips successfully instead of
polling npm until the runner times out. npm publish authority remains isolated to
package `publish-npm` jobs. A skipped package gate must not count as production
deployment for database migrations. For commit-driven selection, the planner checks database-affecting changes against the independent last successful `supabase-production.yaml` migration baseline, not the Platform deployment baseline.
When Platform lacks successful explicit coverage of the target SHA, pending migrations or unavailable migration coverage conservatively select enabled Platform for redeployment; disabled configuration remains authoritative. Ordinary manual dispatch still selects all enabled targets.
Selection retains the successful planner, explicit Platform deployment marker, and exact-SHA completed successful staging requirements. Manual production migration recovery may explicitly set `allow_cloudflare_verification_failures=true` with full matching `expected_sha` and secret-matched `expected_project_ref`: only completed planner failures in the three canonical Cloudflare verifier steps qualify, with all three validations and Platform deployment successful and every other job terminal acceptable. This default-off exception never applies to automatic triggers and never bypasses the current Platform marker, staging gate, normal project secrets or `supabase db push --include-all`; inspect actual application and catalog afterward, without manual SQL.
A registered 15-minute report automation cron is not proof that delivery RPCs are available or email gates are enabled. Missing RPCs remain operational blockers; additive migrations and auto-send toggles do not backfill already-approved reports. Each ready run drains at most five email batches of 20 (100 handled rows) at concurrency four, admitting new batches only within a 30-second budget; already-claimed sends settle before returning, then one generation batch runs. `processedEmails` counts handled queue rows, not Sent or inbox deliveries; `emailBatches` and `emailDrainStopReason` distinguish empty queue, batch limit and admission budget (or missing completion migration). An empty/short claim describes currently eligible rows, not every deferred, locked, blocked or unknown-outcome report.
The marker must explicitly name the platform workflow, deployment kind, and
matching payload SHA, and its latest status must be successful. GitHub
environment records with an empty payload only describe job completion; they
are not deployment evidence. In particular, a package-deferred platform job can
succeed without deploying the API and must never unlock contract-changing
migrations.

`production-package-resume.yaml` listens to completed package releases and successful planner
completions. A failed package-workflow tail still requires live completion agreement
and every exact package version on npm; its conclusion alone proves no publication.
It resumes the owning planner for the exact current production SHA
only when the prior platform job explicitly deferred for package publishing and
all changed package versions are visible on npm. It checks the live completion,
fully paginates planner runs/jobs, and skips active, failed, promoted, or stale candidates. Planner completion also wakes recovery when the
last package became visible before the original planner finished. The dispatch
carries `expected_sha`; the planner skips a recovery if production moves before
it starts. Recovery uses commit-driven deployment-marker and affected-path
selection, including the Cron Control and Devbox Control Workers. An exact-SHA successful deployment marker skips its already covered target,
including Platform, only when its payload explicitly identifies the workflow,
deployment kind, and production ref. Automatic job environment records, build
markers, and a bare marker-SHA override cannot establish recovery coverage. An
older Platform marker still permits package recovery. A known marker
with no affected Worker paths skips them; a missing marker still fails open.
Ordinary operator dispatches continue selecting all enabled targets.
Every snapshotted planner's attempt, status, and conclusion must remain unchanged;
the latest job evidence and run attempt are checked again before reserving an
intent. A completed rerun with the same run ID therefore blocks stale recovery.
Satellite deployments still require the normal verified platform
promotion marker. Completion events use [`queue: max`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#example-queueing-multiple-pending-runs) with cancellation disabled,
so up to 100 completions wait instead of replacing the single pending event;
GitHub cancels overflow beyond that limit. API and npm calls are bounded to
15 seconds each with a four-minute recovery deadline, below the five-minute
job limit. Missing npm visibility and registry read failures retry every two
seconds within that shared deadline, including the final package completion.
Exhaustion fails the recovery job explicitly before creating an intent or
requesting dispatch; it never reports a successful deferred skip. Planner runs
are rechecked after registry reads and immediately before dispatch. GitHub API
timeouts, unreadable/incomplete results, and changed candidates never retry
intent or dispatch writes.
Before dispatch it reserves a durable exact-SHA intent in the dedicated
`production-package-resume` deployment environment with `auto_merge=false`,
empty required contexts, `production_environment=false`, and
`transient_environment=true`. This is a dispatch lock, not deployment or
migration evidence: no success status is emitted and the real platform marker
still uses `vercel-production-platform`. Each dispatch passes the returned reservation ID as `resume_intent`; the planner's
run-name binds that ID and exact SHA. An existing intent blocks subsequent
completions until its uniquely bound planner is proven completed successfully,
package-deferred, and unpromoted. If npm visibility failed again, a later completion
may reserve a new intent only after all prior intents have that proof, current
versions are visible, and fresh intent/run/attempt/job/ref snapshots agree.
Legacy or unbound intents, absent runs, failed, uncertain, or timed-out requests
remain blocked for operator inspection. Intents are never deleted; the exact-SHA
recovery concurrency group serializes reservation, and a changed intent set blocks
the next write. This
requires `deployments: write` only in the recovery workflow.
A deferred successful workflow is not deployment evidence.
Validate this guard with `node --test scripts/ci/resume-production-package-deployment*.test.js`.

The gate queries the planner run because reusable app workflows do not create
standalone Actions runs.

Filtered production Docker installs only include the selected app and the
dependencies that app needs. Workspace packages with direct `tsc` build scripts
must declare `typescript` in their own `devDependencies`; do not
rely on the root devDependency for production Docker builds. Programmatic
compiler API consumers must stay on the active TypeScript 7 toolchain instead
of carrying legacy compiler compatibility packages.

Next.js production apps also declare `@typescript/native-preview` in their own
`devDependencies` while the repo uses the TypeScript 7 native compiler package.
The TS7 `typescript` package does not ship the legacy
`typescript/lib/typescript.js` API file that Next checks during build-time
TypeScript setup; the native-preview marker makes Next use its supported TS7
native compiler path instead of trying to auto-install classic TypeScript.

### Superseded-run guards

Production Vercel workflows use a static per-app concurrency prefix and Git ref
with a `cancel-in-progress` predicate restricted to push events on
`refs/heads/production`. A newer production push cancels only the older run for
that same app instead of cancelling sibling app deployments or allowing an
obsolete run to finish green. A `main` commit or manual recovery dispatch does
not cancel the running production deploy. The newest production run stays queued
or active and deploys the cumulative branch state.

Deployment markers still let affected-app gating compare every change since
the last successful deployment, including changes accumulated across canceled
intermediate runs. If the marker is missing or cannot be trusted, Vercel gating
defaults open so a later unrelated commit cannot hide an earlier app change.

### Prerequisite guards

- `supabase-staging.yaml` requires a successful same-repository `push` platform
  preview build on `main` unless manually dispatched from `main`; its checkout-local `ci`
  boolean must enable it. Changing the file changes its Git blob. In the same
  change, update every pin of that blob:
  - the producer-contract allowlist in `supabase-production.yaml`;
  - `scripts/ci/production-migration-target.test.js`;
  - `scripts/ci/staging-contract-allowlist.test.js`, which pins the exact list
    and requires the current blob as the last entry.

  Keep the list to the current blob plus blobs from `main`'s history, and drop
  blobs from rejected or intermediate branch heads.
  `bun check:changed` runs these contract tests whenever a pinned producer file
  changes, but it is no substitute for the exact-head CI result before merge.
- Every enabled admitted target, including app-only commits, links staging and runs
  `supabase db push --include-all` before emitting its exact-target marker. The
  exception is a target whose migrations a descendant `main` commit has already
  applied, with staging ahead only by `main`'s versions. It records the marker
  without pushing. A staging version that is not on `main` fails closed.
- `supabase-production.yaml` runs after the production deployment planner and
  also re-evaluates the current immutable `production` commit after any successful
  `main` staging migration. The staging event's incoming SHA may be newer and
  unpromoted, so it does not become the production migration target. Target
  resolution precedes checkout. Staging proof binds the newest exact-source marker,
  latest success, allowlisted rehashed contracts and current attempt's actual apply/marker; target/wrapper may use different reviewed contracts. Manual dispatch stays on `production`; planner completions
  remain pinned to their successful production run's SHA. The workflow still
  requires that target's successful planner result, production platform deployment
  marker, and source-bound staging proof before `supabase db push --include-all`.
  Failed, cancelled and other non-success
  workflow callbacks skip before allocating the evaluation job and use a unique
  ignored-run concurrency group. Successful callbacks from mismatched workflow/branch
  pairs and manual dispatches outside `refs/heads/production` are isolated the same
  way, so they cannot replace a legitimate pending migration. Only successful
  production-planner/production and staging/main callbacks, plus manual production
  branch runs, retain the global migration group with active-run cancellation disabled.

### Mobile iOS native assets

Mobile workflows use `.github/actions/setup-flutter-with-cache` for Flutter
SDK/pub downloads (Windows retains its deliberate cache-off setup). The wrapper
resolves identity through the SHA-pinned upstream action before restoring the
exact cache, then installs that resolved version. SDK keys bind upstream OS,
channel, version, architecture and release hash; they exclude `pubspec.lock` so
analysis, test and build jobs share main's SDK archive. Pub download keys
(`flutter-pub-v2-`) also exclude the lock hash. Every ref can restore; only main push/manual runs attach
the cache save post-step, so mobile runs on PRs, feature branches and
production do not upload duplicate archives. Desktop beta/store-draft and the
employee schema contract still set up Flutter with upstream caching on their own
triggers; move them to the wrapper before relying on main-only Flutter saves
repository-wide. Pub downloads save after job work, preserving `pub get`
results. Bun's existing setup helper already uses trusted main saves.

These caches share repository capacity with Supabase image archives. This policy
reduces duplicate writes; it does not remove existing entries, raise the storage
limit or guarantee image retention. Observe exact main image-cache keys and sizes
after seeding and again after the normal CI wave.

Android workflows also use the toolchain-aware Gradle cache, and iOS or
macOS workflows cache CocoaPods downloads plus the trunk repository. They do
not cache `apps/mobile/build`, final APK/AAB/IPA/app bundles, `Pods`, or
`apps/mobile/.dart_tool`. Flutter native asset hook outputs can become stale
across simulator/device builds and SDK updates; a stale `.dart_tool` cache can
leave `NativeAssetsManifest.json` referencing `objective_c` while
`build/native_assets/ios/` is missing the generated framework.

Every workflow still runs `flutter pub get` and its platform build on every run.
Development deliverables are retained for 7 days and production store
deliverables for 14 days. Archive directory-based app bundles before upload,
disable redundant artifact compression for already-compressed archives and
mobile packages, and fail if a required deliverable is missing.

The workflow explicitly runs `flutter config --no-enable-swift-package-manager`
after Flutter setup. Keep the iOS CI path on CocoaPods while `image_cropper` and
`dkimagepickercontroller` resolve incompatible `TOCropViewController` Swift
package ranges; otherwise Flutter 3.44+ can fail before the simulator build
with an Xcode package dependency resolution error.

The iOS/macOS build workflows currently resolve `macos-latest` to GitHub's
macOS 26 ARM64 image with Xcode 26+. The former Xcode 16.4 compatibility pins
for `connectivity_plus` and `device_info_plus` are no longer required. Before
adding a future Apple-specific dependency pin, verify the active runner image
from a build log and reproduce the native build failure on that toolchain.

### Mobile store beta deployment

`mobile-deploy-stores.yaml` runs automatically on `production` pushes that touch
`apps/mobile/**`, `scripts/mobile-deployment/**`, the workflow file,
`ci-check.yml`, or `tuturuuu.ts`. It is a beta-store workflow only:

- Android builds the production flavor AAB from `apps/mobile/.env.github` and
  publishes it to the Google Play `internal` track.
- iOS builds the production flavor IPA from `apps/mobile/.env.github` and
  uploads it to TestFlight.
- The iOS job verifies the signed local IPA before upload. It also tries to
  retain an IPA artifact for debugging, but a GitHub artifact storage timeout
  does not stop the TestFlight upload or beta-group verification.
- CI requests a signed GitHub OIDC token for the
  `tuturuuu-mobile-deployment` audience, then fetches an Android or iOS bundle
  from `https://infrastructure.tuturuuu.com/api/v1/mobile-deployment/bundle` with the issued
  `MOBILE_DEPLOYMENT_CI_TOKEN`.
- If `MOBILE_DEPLOYMENT_CI_TOKEN` is not configured in the `mobile-store-beta`
  GitHub Environment, the credentials preflight fails. Android and iOS publish
  only after that preflight succeeds. Do not pass a credential-presence flag as a
  job output: GitHub may redact it as secret-like, silently skipping both jobs.
  An invalid token fails during the bundle fetch.
- The apps/web mobile deployment vault verifies the CI token, GitHub OIDC
  issuer, audience, repository, `production` ref, workflow file, and
  `mobile-store-beta` environment before returning any plaintext.
- CI hydrates ignored Firebase, signing, store, and `.env.github` files into
  fixed paths under `apps/mobile` and `$RUNNER_TEMP` with `umask 077`, validates
  plaintext SHA-256 hashes, masks secret values, and deletes generated files in
  `always()` cleanup steps.
- The workflow rejects any Google Play track other than `internal`, uploads only
  the AAB/IPA build artifacts, and uses TestFlight-only iOS upload.
- The workflow uses the greater of the `apps/mobile/pubspec.yaml` patch and
  one patch above matching iOS pre-release versions in App Store Connect.
  With `0.11.0+84` and no matching history, the first upload is `0.11.0`;
  subsequent uploads advance to `0.11.1`, then `0.11.2`. An unused higher
  source patch is retained. It calculates a separate build
  number from `GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER` and `GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT`; both stores receive
  the same version name. The iOS publish job resolves that version after its
  single vault bundle fetch; Android waits for the nonsecret version output.
  Do not fetch the iOS bundle in preflight as well: the vault rejects a second
  fetch for the same run attempt as a replay.

The workflow is bound to the `mobile-store-beta` GitHub Environment. Keep that
environment restricted to the `production` branch and store only
`MOBILE_DEPLOYMENT_CI_TOKEN` there. Mobile signing, Firebase, store API, and
build-time secrets live in the root workspace mobile deployment vault at
`/internal/mobile-deployment` on the infra app and require
`manage_mobile_deployment_vault`. Manage non-file values in the vault's
**Secrets** panel, then use the vault's Verify action before activating the draft. Legacy
base64 file payload env keys are intentionally blocked; Firebase, signing, and
store credential payloads must be uploaded as file resources.

Local release-build verification should run before relying on the workflow:

```sh
bun test scripts/ci/check-workflow-config.test.js
ruby -e "require 'yaml'; YAML.load_file('.github/workflows/mobile-deploy-stores.yaml')"
git diff --check
bun check:mobile
(cd apps/mobile && flutter pub get)
(cd apps/mobile && flutter build appbundle --release --flavor production --target lib/main_production.dart --dart-define-from-file=.env.github)
```

iOS IPA verification requires full Xcode, not only Command Line Tools:

```sh
xcodebuild -version
(cd apps/mobile && flutter config --no-enable-swift-package-manager)
(cd apps/mobile && flutter build ipa --release --flavor production --target lib/main_production.dart --dart-define-from-file=.env.github)
```

If `xcodebuild -version` reports that Command Line Tools are selected, switch to
full Xcode before claiming the iOS archive has been verified locally.

## Fast Triage Checklist

1. Check whether `ci-check.yml` disabled the workflow through `tuturuuu.ts`.
2. For Vercel workflows, inspect the `ci-check.yml` decision reason and matched paths.
3. Inspect the changed-file source, base SHA, head SHA, and path count emitted by
   `resolve-changed-files.ts`.
4. Check whether the workflow was canceled because a newer run superseded it,
   then follow the newest run in the same workflow-and-branch concurrency group.
5. Check whether the prior successful GitHub Deployment marker exists for that
   Vercel workflow and branch.
6. Check path filters to confirm GitHub should have started the lightweight workflow.
7. For database workflows, inspect the prerequisite evaluation job before the deploy job.
8. Docker setup CI is paused; retained Docker steps are not current release gates.

## When You Add New Automation

1. Add the workflow file under `.github/workflows/`.
2. Add its key to `tuturuuu.ts` unless you intentionally want it always on by default.
3. Document the workflow in `apps/docs`.
4. If it changes a docs-visible page, add that page to `apps/docs/docs.json`.

### Calendar retained generation rollout

The `calendar-generation-contract.yaml` workflow applies every migration in a
throwaway local Supabase project, runs strict Calendar pgTAP fixtures, generates
RPC types from that database, and removes its own project. Its artifact names
include the exact source SHA. Run the same finite contract with
`node apps/database/scripts/verify-calendar-generation-contract.mjs` only when
local Docker is healthy and the resource queue admits the validation.

The compatibility guard migration must reach production before deploying any
Calendar code that consumes the provider operation ledger. First ship the guard
without a ledger or feature activation, verify the automated production migration,
then ship dependent Calendar changes. App deployment precedes production
migrations; an absent RPC or API schema cache is not proof that a ledger is absent.
The guard checks actual PostgreSQL relation presence and fails closed on partial
or incompatible ledger schemas. Never replace a missing guard with an unguarded
provider write.

### i18n PR report evidence

The i18n report requires both a completed job result and its explicit validator
output. Cancelled, skipped, missing-output, and contradictory results are reported
as incomplete; they establish neither a translation defect nor passing validation.
Only confirmed validator failures offer repair commands. Reports identify the
source head and workflow run. Comment writes are serialized per PR, paginate all
existing comments, reject superseded heads, and preserve newer run/attempt reports.
A branch can still advance after the final API head check; the embedded source
identity makes that evidence boundary visible. Existing cancelled job conclusions
are unchanged. Regression coverage: `node --test scripts/ci/i18n-report.test.js`.


## Pending concurrency, skips and exact-head receipts

`cancel-in-progress: false` protects a running workflow; it does not preserve the
default single pending slot. A new run in the same group replaces the previous
pending run. GitHub now supports `queue: max` for up to 100 pending runs when
cancellation is disabled. See the [official concurrency syntax](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#concurrency).
This is an available mechanism, not proof that every repository workflow uses it.

Choose the group from the workload: validation can use workflow/event/commit
identity; deployments that mutate the same environment still need serialization.
Do not make deployment groups unique merely to remove cancellation badges. A
valid duplicate should reach the repository's proof-based skip decision. Failure,
missing outputs or unavailable proof must run validation rather than silently
skip it. Queue saturation can still cancel new runs; inspect the recorded reason.

For an integration receipt, query the full exact SHA directly:

```bash
gh api "repos/tutur3u/platform/actions/runs?head_sha=$CANDIDATE_SHA&per_page=100"
gh api "repos/tutur3u/platform/commits/$CANDIDATE_SHA/check-runs?per_page=100"
```

Follow pagination. A branch listing, old green notification or PR summary can
refer to an earlier head. Verify every returned `head_sha`, include late fan-out
and separately inspect deployment/migration markers. A queued, cancelled or
missing required workflow is not a successful delivery receipt.

### Diagnose image uploads before widening browser deadlines

A small PNG that has a valid signature and dimensions can still contain a bad
chunk checksum. Client-side optimization may fail during pixel decoding before
an upload-ticket request is sent. Trace the last entered browser operation and
whether the ticket endpoint was requested, then decode the exact synthetic
fixture with the same image-processing boundary. Do not infer a server upload
failure from an absent request or simply widen the browser assertion timeout.

The shared fixture in `apps/web/e2e/helpers/profile-media-fixture.ts` is exercised
by `scripts/ci/profile-media-fixture.test.js`: pixel decoding and bounded WebP
optimization succeed, while a corrupt checksum fails. These checks establish the
fixture contract, not browser or provider upload success. Confirm the real
request -> upload -> save -> reload path separately.

### Preserve causal E2E failures and owned process lifecycle

Public Playwright discovery receipts must preserve project dependencies and the
original test selection. Diagnostic stdout may surround JSON; parse a validated
report shape, and retain a safe original-selection fallback when discovery is
unavailable. Never evaluate private Playwright bundles to reconstruct behavior.

Detached satellite process groups require explicit cleanup on timeout and runner
signals. Track only groups the current invocation created, remove them only after
cleanup is confirmed, and preserve the runner's signal exit semantics. Child
`exit` alone does not establish that descendants or stdout have closed. Wait for
`close` when checking terminal output and wait for a fixture's readiness receipt
before testing its TERM handler under concurrent load.

When report merging also fails after a failed cohort, preserve the original test
failure as the primary cause and attach the merge failure as diagnostics. A
standalone report-merge failure remains a failure. Test these lifecycle boundaries
with real owned child processes and synthetic failures; helper-only source checks
are not proof that a stalled browser process exits.

## Superseded validation and production runner admission

PR validation uses workflow, event and PR number with `cancel-in-progress` enabled.
A new head replaces older queued or running validation for that PR. PR-target
workflows use the PR identity because their Git ref is the base branch. Safe
push-to-main validation uses workflow and ref rather than SHA, so newer main
commits replace obsolete validation. Production, generated Release Please refs and
manual validation and rerun attempts keep independent immutable groups. Attempts
with `github.run_attempt > 1` disable cancellation and include SHA, run ID and
attempt in their group. Later main pushes cannot share that group; rerunning a
candidate also cannot cancel current main validation.

Only the exact SHA selected for production promotion needs complete CI.
Superseded main SHAs do not each need a full green receipt. A cancelled workflow
is never a passing check or a valid duplicate proof. If an authorized pinned
candidate lost required validation to a later main push, rerun the missing checks
for that exact candidate before promotion. Newer-head green checks cannot replace
that evidence. The existing exact-SHA promotion gate remains mandatory.

To qualify a pinned candidate, select the existing run by its exact full SHA and
workflow, verify its identity, and rerun that run (all jobs, not only failures):

```sh
candidate_sha=<authorized-full-sha>
gh run list --repo tutur3u/platform --commit "$candidate_sha" \
  --workflow type-check.yaml --json databaseId,headSha,event,status,conclusion
candidate_run=<verified-run-id>
gh run view "$candidate_run" --repo tutur3u/platform \
  --json headSha,headBranch,event,attempt,workflowName
gh run rerun "$candidate_run" --repo tutur3u/platform
```

Repeat for every missing required workflow. Confirm the selected run's `headSha`
equals the authorized candidate before rerunning, then inspect its new attempt and
all required job conclusions after completion. GitHub reruns retain the original
SHA/ref; they remain push events and use the protected rerun group. A workflow
with `workflow_dispatch` also has an isolated SHA/run/attempt group, but dispatching
`--ref main` resolves current main and does not qualify an older candidate.

This protection requires the workflow revision used by the run to contain this
policy. Rerunning an older workflow revision does not backport the policy. If the
candidate has no run with this protection, stop promotion and obtain an authorized
qualification path for that exact source; do not substitute newer-head evidence.

The explicit PR exceptions are `desktop-beta.yaml`, whose production build and
publication share the workflow lock; `calendar-cloudflare.yaml` and
`mail-cloudflare.yaml`, whose staging publication consumes the durable attempt
ledger; `playground-runtime-acceptance.yaml`, which must finish real sandbox
cleanup; and the paused `docker-setup-check.yaml` and `rust-backend.yml`.

The Colab, Coordination, Cron Control, Devbox Control, Lettin, Meet and Parley
Cloudflare workflows are not exceptions. Their workflow-level group uses the
standard validation policy with a literal per-workflow prefix, so PR and `main`
validation supersede older revisions. The prefix matters because a
`workflow_call` run inherits the caller's `github.workflow`; without it, the
workflows one production planner run calls would share a group and replace each
other's pending runs. Only the production-gated `deploy` job holds the
serialized lock: a static `<workflow>-production-deploy` job group with
cancellation disabled and `queue: max`. Production and manual runs keep unique
workflow groups. `scripts/ci/protected-workflow-concurrency.test.js` pins this
split. The paused
`tanstack-route-manifest.yaml` retains its existing PR supersession and protected
main policy. Resuming a paused runtime requires a separate policy review.

Mutating production planners, production Vercel and Cloudflare deployments, database
migrations, package publication, Release Please and store deployments retain their
shared serialization groups with cancellation disabled and `queue: max`.
Discord Modal deployment holds its lock on the success/main-guarded deploy job;
cancelled CI completions never enter that lock. It accepts only same-repository
`push` completions on `main` or manual dispatch from `main`, and runs in the
`discord-production` environment (give it a `main`-only branch policy and the
Modal secrets). Biome has no workflow-level
cancelling parent: check/config/format/lint jobs cancel by job and ref, while
format PR creation, PR closure/branch deletion and comment writes share a separate
non-cancelling `biome-mutations-<ref>` job group with `queue: max`.
[GitHub concurrency](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#concurrency)
allows up to 100 pending runs in these groups. Queue overflow can still cancel
excess runs. Queue order reflects when each run began waiting, so existing target
relevance and deployment-marker guards remain authoritative. `queue: max` must
never be combined with cancellation enabled.

The production planner already uses a dedicated serialization group and resolves
all app configurations in one process. Vercel app workflows run directly without
separate config jobs. Cloudflare app workflows still check configuration and run
validation before deployment. Meet, Lettin and Parley now fold PR release-only
checks into that existing config job, removing up to three runner allocations per
production plan. The check preserves PR base/head comparison and returns true for
production and manual runs. No validation or deployment job is removed.

Concurrency groups do not reserve runner capacity or prioritize production over
PR jobs on GitHub-hosted runners. Removing obsolete validation and redundant gate
jobs reduces demand but does not establish a queue-time improvement. Further
consolidation needs equivalent per-app configuration outputs and failure handling.
A dedicated runner pool or more account capacity needs separate infrastructure
ownership. Upskii's Linux runners are not available for Tuturuuu jobs.

These policies apply to new workflow runs after the change reaches the applicable
workflow ref. They do not clean an already queued backlog or cancel merged PR runs
without another event. Existing-run cleanup remains a separate authorized action.

Regression coverage: `scripts/ci/protected-workflow-concurrency.test.js` discovers
all PR and main-push workflows, checks supersession and explicit exceptions, and
checks isolated rerun/dispatch groups, discovers workflow-run consumers and
preserves mutating locks, including Biome jobs and Modal deployment. These are
source/expression regressions, not a hosted scheduler or deployment experiment.
Workflow-local contracts also inspect YAML outside `scripts/ci`; root script
discovery does not cover every database suite. Run each workflow's Node contract
tests after concurrency changes. For example,
`node --test apps/database/scripts/topic-delivery-foundation-contract.test.mjs`
checks main/PR supersession, non-cancelling production/release-please pushes,
SHA/run/attempt isolation for protected pushes, reruns and dispatches, and negative
controls for the former main policy and missing isolation guards.
`scripts/ci/production-preflight-consolidation.test.js`
executes the shared PR release check and validates the reduced job graph. Meet
validation also depends on the production policy: consolidation reads both
`should_run` and `run_checks` from `check-ci` while retaining explicit successful
policy admission before production credentials can be used. A skipped policy on
PR/main must not skip validation; a failed or held production policy must block it.
Credential regressions live in `scripts/ci/production-publisher-secrets.test.js`.


### PR runner pool: variable, canary and kill switch

Selected PR checks can run on a dedicated self-hosted macOS pool. Routing is off
unless the repository Actions variable `PR_SELF_HOSTED_RUNNERS` is set:

| Value | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| unset, empty or `false` | Off (kill switch): every job uses `ubuntu-latest`. |
| `pr:<number>` | Canary: only pull request `<number>` routes to the pool. |
| `true` | On: every eligible pull request routes to the pool. |

A job routes only for a `pull_request` event whose head branch is in this
repository (no forks), with a non-Dependabot author, actor and triggering actor,
on the single label `tuturuuu-pr-ephemeral` (`self-hosted, macOS, ARM64`). The
label `tuturuuu-mac-studio` is never selected. Push, dispatch,
`pull_request_target` and reusable-workflow contexts stay on `ubuntu-latest`.
Routing never replaces the `ready-for-ci` gate.

Routed jobs: `docs-seo-check.yaml` `validate`; `i18n-check.yaml`
`i18n-sort-check`, `i18n-translation-check`, `i18n-key-parity-check` and
`i18n-namespace-check`; `mobile-api-mappings.yaml` `verify`; `type-check.yaml`
`type-check-pr`; `biome-check.yaml` `check-ci` (through the `pr_runner` input of
`ci-check.yml`), `duplicate-validation`, `format` and `lint`;
`turbo-unit-tests.yaml` `test-shards-pr`. Jobs with write tokens (Biome apply,
close and comment jobs, the i18n comment job), the Codecov upload and every
secret-bearing, deploy, release, migration or security job stay on
`ubuntu-latest`. Pool jobs get no secrets, and the pool has no ambient
credentials. GitHub ships every secret a job names to its runner even when a
guard such as `github.event_name != 'pull_request'` evaluates to an empty
string, so a pool-eligible job must not contain the substring `secrets.` at all
(no guarded credential expressions), and a reusable workflow it calls receives no
secrets.

Type Check and the unit-test shards still need Turbo and Supabase credentials on
push and dispatch, so each is split into two jobs that share one `name` and
therefore one required check context: `type-check-pr` and `test-shards-pr` run
only for `pull_request` events, may route to the pool and use fixtures or empty
values; `type-check` and `test-shards` run only for other events on
`ubuntu-latest` and keep their secrets. Exactly one of each pair runs, the other
reports as skipped. Dependents of `test-shards` (`coverage-shards`,
`coverage-upload`, `coverage-result`, `Unit Tests (24)`) need both variants and
read the result of whichever one ran (the other is skipped), so a skipped variant
never masks a failed one.
`scripts/ci/workflow-pr-self-hosted.test.js` asserts that the raw text of every
job able to select the pool has no `secrets.` substring and that the reusable
workflows such jobs call take no secrets.

Each routed job checks out without persisted credentials, runs
`./.github/actions/pr-runner-hygiene` (disposable `HOME`, Git, Bun, npm and XDG
state, `npm_config_ignore_scripts=true`) and installs with
`bun install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts`. Build and generation steps run
explicitly from repository scripts, never from dependency lifecycle scripts. The
action's post step (`post-if: always()`) empties the workspace and removes the
job state. Caches are restored on pull requests and saved only by trusted
non-PR runs.

Canary procedure:

1. Confirm the pool runners exist and carry only the `tuturuuu-pr-ephemeral`
   label.
2. Run `gh variable set PR_SELF_HOSTED_RUNNERS --repo tutur3u/platform --body 'pr:<number>'`.
3. Push a commit to that pull request (new assignments only) and inspect the
   exact-head jobs with `gh api repos/tutur3u/platform/actions/runs/<run-id>/jobs`:
   runner labels, queue and execution time, conclusions.
4. Widen to `true` only after the canary is clean.

Kill switch: `gh variable delete PR_SELF_HOSTED_RUNNERS --repo tutur3u/platform`
(or set `false`). New assignments fall back to hosted immediately; jobs already
assigned keep running and need to be cancelled by run.

The label-only pool split is an interim control. Allow at most 72 hours from the
time the variable is first set to a value other than off: if a separate macOS
user for the runners is not in place by then, unset the variable. Cleanup is not
a sandbox; it does not stop malicious same-repository code from affecting the
runner's service user.

Regression coverage: `scripts/ci/workflow-pr-self-hosted.test.js` and
`.github/actions/pr-runner-hygiene/index.test.js`.

### Calendar scheduling startup requests

The Calendar priority panel reads per-user scheduling summaries through the Tasks
batch API, using at most 100 distinct task IDs per request and sequential chunks.
This replaces one HTTP request per task. The verified actor, calendar workspace,
and source-task membership are checked before settings or event data are returned;
personal mode counts events only in the personal calendar. Event pages must all
succeed before a snapshot is published. Linked and directly associated events are
deduplicated by task and event ID.

The client retains the last snapshot during transient revalidation, clears visible
summaries on definitive access denial, and refreshes stale data on window focus.
This scope is scheduling summaries, not the whole Calendar startup waterfall.
Regression coverage lives in `task-schedule-batch.test.ts` and
`tasks-scheduling-batch.test.ts`. Measure authenticated navigation and meaningful
content after the exact source is deployed; local checks alone are not latency proof.

### Devbox Control Vite-native artifact

Devbox Control owns a private workspace with Vite+ and scoped Oxlint/Oxfmt
configuration. The workspace pins Wrangler 4.149.0 so local runtime checks
support the retained compatibility date; root Wrangler is not the runtime oracle
for this scope. The Cloudflare Vite plugin emits `apps/devbox-control/dist/worker`
from the existing Wrangler configuration; Worker name, account, compatibility,
RunnerWake class/binding/migration and required secret names remain the source
configuration's authority. No Supabase auth, runner membership, lease, heartbeat,
notification or WebSocket policy changes accompany tooling adoption.

CI generates Worker types, checks TypeScript and scoped Oxc rules, and runs the
existing 13 authorization/protocol tests through Vite+. Before and after the
real Vite build, `node --test apps/devbox-control/scripts/verify-worker-runtime.mjs`
checks complete health JSON and rejects unauthenticated runner/internal requests
in a loopback Worker with disposable secrets. Set `DEVBOX_TEST_CONFIG` to an
absolute emitted `dist/worker/wrangler.json` path for artifact verification.
Dry-run bundling and the authorized production job consume that emitted config;
secret provisioning still uses the unchanged source target identity.

The fixture closes its temporary runtime and does not contact Supabase or hosted
runners. It proves Worker startup and denial-before-remote-access, not successful
real-account authentication, RunnerWake WebSocket delivery or hosted lease
transitions. Those remain separate acceptance evidence before canonical migration.
Release builds run only in exact-commit CI. Locally, queue lint/types/unit/runtime
checks with `ttr resources run`; use a private writable TMPDIR when shared temporary
storage rejects writes. The format command checks only owned source and remains
read-only; existing Biome gates remain authoritative until formatter/rule parity.

This tooling unit adds no alarm, queue, retry chain, storage operation or scheduler.
Review background-work and operation-cost bounds separately when those paths change;
health and build success do not establish a spending cap or production promotion.

#### RunnerWake notification operation envelope

The current RunnerWake class performs no alarm, queue or cron rescheduling. A
successful internal POST enumerates all retained WebSockets and sends one wake to
each. For `S` retained sockets and `N` duplicate notifications, count `N × S` send
attempts; failed sends also attempt a close. No durable progress receipt suppresses
later duplicate fanout. A throwing close aborts remaining delivery and propagates
failure rather than returning a complete acknowledgement.

The public notify route authenticates the internal token before one run lookup,
an optional lease lookup and one Durable Object POST. Connect authenticates the
runner before forwarding the WebSocket upgrade. The object trusts these forwarding
boundaries; it does not establish an independent durable stop fence or socket lease.
These per-request counts do not bound retained sockets, repeated ingress, billed
messages, downstream query rows or total account spend.

`apps/devbox-control/src/wake.test.ts` counts 98,304 sends for 4,096 synthetic sockets
and 24 duplicate/reconstructed notifications, then checks failed-send closure and
incomplete fanout on a throwing close. These tests use the actual class with a
mocked Durable Object base and sockets. They do not verify hosted WebSocket delivery,
provider billing, authenticated Stop or real persisted leases. Before amplifying
this path, require bounded per-wake work, an expiring recurring authority and a
durable authenticated stop fence, preserving recovery and notification semantics.


### Native Vite+ test and coverage version alignment

Vite+ 1.1.0 requires Vitest and coverage-v8 5.0.3 together. Pin the root dependency,
root `vitest` override and provider with Bun; an older root override replaces
Vite+'s declared runner even when ordinary tests pass. The coverage guard rejects
that mismatch rather than producing unreliable coverage. Shared CI forwards
`--maxWorkers=2` and optionally `--coverage`: keep worker/pool defaults in the
unit config, not a duplicate CLI flag in package scripts. Validate both forwarded
commands under Node 24 in the owning workspace through `ttr resources`.

### Playground metadata lifecycle evidence

The disposable Playground acceptance job opts into the SDK's
`TTR_DOCKER_METADATA_DIAGNOSTIC=1` diagnostic. See the
[SDK diagnostic contract](/reference/packages/sdk#docker-metadata-lifecycle-diagnostic).
Read each `ttr-docker-metadata-v1` record with its exact commit, job and invocation
ordinal. Event times describe JavaScript observations on the same existing
metadata subprocess; null close timing does not prove that the process failed to
close later. Callback lateness measures delay relative to the scheduled deadline.
There is no extra Docker probe, warmup, retry or deadline increase.

An instrumented passing run provides observability only: it cannot explain a
historical timeout. A timer callback proves deadline classification before
settlement, not daemon failure or a Node/Bun adapter defect. Keep causal diagnosis
UNKNOWN until same-invocation evidence distinguishes those hypotheses; source
review and mock tests do not qualify hosted runtime acceptance.

## Report-only Web E2E

The sole Docker exception is `.github/workflows/e2e-smoke-report-only.yaml`:
trusted main pushes run Web browser smoke; the nightly schedule runs the full
non-quarantined Web browser suite at 19:17 UTC. Manual main dispatch runs smoke.
A temporary CLI compatibility launcher forwards retained helpers' `bunx` calls
to `bun x`; dependency installation uses the repository retry helper.
The user authorized this workflow-specific exception on 2026-10-28. Existing
disabled E2E/image/setup jobs, general Docker commands, Rust, TanStack, and the
Docker cron runner remain paused. This is CI browser verification, not a
deployment or permission to run arbitrary Docker tasks.

The three Chromium smoke tests cover login rendering, seeded password sign-in,
and signup through team onboarding, workspace, board, and persisted task creation.
The full lifecycle test retains invitation and Kanban CRUD coverage. Collect
from Web with `bunx playwright test --list --grep @smoke --grep-invert @quarantine`.
The target is at most six minutes of Playwright time, enforced with a 330-second
global budget and no retries. Provisioning is separate and can require image
builds and database setup; total runtime is not yet measured. The nightly
Playwright budget is 40 minutes.

The registered fleet labels are `self-hosted, macOS, ARM64,
tuturuuu-mac-studio`. There is no FLEET-labelled workflow template on main.
The scoped `scripts/ci/run-web-e2e-report-only.js` launcher admits only this
workflow at main on a self-hosted Mac. It calls the retained launcher directly;
the general package aliases still refuse execution. Rust backend, native host
builds, global BuildKit pruning, and the cron runner are forced off. Only Next
and the services/satellites required by its browser fixtures run.

### Fleet isolation and recovery

Each run uses unique Compose and Supabase project identities and private
`PORTLESS_STATE_DIR` state. The retained TLS-marker cleanup honors that private
directory. A host lock at `~/.tuturuuu/ci-web-e2e.lock` serializes these jobs
across runner registrations and event types. An already busy Docker daemon or
required local port fails admission before any existing runtime is touched.
Such a failure is diagnostic, not a green or skipped smoke result.

Ordinary pushes supersede older ordinary pushes. Manual dispatches and reruns
use distinct immutable concurrency groups. The host lock additionally protects
fixed local auth origins across those groups. The always-running cleanup step
checks the lock's run/attempt/workspace identity before stopping only its own
Compose project, Supabase fixture and private Portless proxy. Cleanup failure
retains the lock. After an interrupted runner, the CI owner must inspect
`owner.json`, verify/stop the identified resources, and verify no fixture
processes or containers remain before removing that specific stale lock.
Do not automatically steal locks, kill unrelated workloads, or globally prune
Docker to recover capacity.

### Observation, quarantine and graduation

The job is report-only with `continue-on-error: true` and must remain outside
branch protection during the first observation week. Its summary records the
actual smoke/nightly/cleanup step outcomes. Seven-day HTML reports and failure
traces are uploaded on every outcome when available. Use only disposable local
fixtures and inspect trace content before sharing. A green workflow wrapper
alone does not establish a successful browser run; inspect the step outcomes.

Append `@quarantine` to a flaky test title, retaining `@smoke` when applicable.
Both commands exclude that tag. File one GitHub issue per quarantined test with
its file and exact title, failing run/artifact link, observed failure, reproduction
command, owner, and a review date within seven days. Link the issue in a nearby
test comment. Fix the cause, verify repeated real runs, then remove the tag and
close the issue. Do not quarantine setup failures or the entire suite.
Collect quarantined tests with `bunx playwright test --list --grep @quarantine`.

The observation week begins with the first successful enabled run. After seven
consecutive days of green smoke runs, propose making smoke required in a separate
reviewed change with exact-head reports, measured runtime, flake/quarantine
inventory, and branch-protection approval. Missing, skipped, busy-runner, timed-out,
or failed-cleanup runs do not count green. Nightly remains diagnostic.

## Frozen workflow installs and release credentials

Workflow dependency installs use `bun install --frozen-lockfile`. The retry
helper adds the flag for project installs; workflows also state it explicitly.
Deliberate lockfile regeneration and pinned global CLI installs must match an
exact workflow file, step name and full command in
`scripts/ci/frozen-bun-install-exceptions.json`. Every exception disables lifecycle
scripts with `--ignore-scripts`; lockfile rewrites also use `--lockfile-only`.
An immediately preceding `# unfrozen-bun-install: <reason>` comment documents
the exception but grants no exemption. Copied markers outside the allowlist fail.
Run `node --test scripts/ci/frozen-bun-install-guard.test.js` to check the policy.

Release Please and Biome checks run the Biome binary from the frozen dependency
install with lifecycle scripts disabled. Release Please installs from the trusted
production checkout before switching to generated content, disables checkout
credential persistence, and passes Git push credentials only to push steps.
The checkout-credentials and generated-format tests cover those boundaries.

The pre-existing overflow-recovery and generated-description Node scripts still
receive the admin token in their step environments. Removing that exposure is
a separate SR-393 follow-up; disabling persisted Git credentials does not close it.
